name: Exodus
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: Here are the names of Israel’s sons who traveled to Egypt with Jacob, each bringing his own family:
They were Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah,
along with Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,
and also Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.
Jacob’s own descendants numbered seventy people.{a} Joseph was in Egypt already.
In time Joseph died, and so did all of his brothers and everyone else of that generation.
The Israelites, though, kept having children. They swarmed{b} across the land and grew so powerful that the whole region was crowded with them.
Then a new king took the throne of Egypt, one who had never known Joseph.
He told his people, “These Israelites are becoming too many and too strong for us.
We need a clever plan. If they keep multiplying, they might side with our enemies in a war, fight against us, and leave the country.”
So the Egyptians appointed slave drivers to crush the Israelites with hard labor. The Israelites built two cities, Pithom and Rameses,{c} to store the supplies of Pharaoh.{d}
But the harder the Egyptians pushed them, the faster the Israelites grew and spread out, and the Egyptians began to dread them.
They drove the Israelites mercilessly in their work.
Life turned bitter for God’s people. They mixed mortar, made bricks, and did all kinds of farm labor, and the Egyptians showed no mercy in any of it.
Next the king of Egypt gave orders to two Hebrew midwives, whose names were Shiphrah and Puah.{e}
“When you attend a Hebrew mother at the birthing stones,{f}” he told them, “check the newborn. A boy must be killed, but a girl may live.”
The midwives respected God too much to obey the king of Egypt, so they let the boys live.
The king called them in and demanded, “Why have you done this? Why are the boys still alive?”
The midwives told Pharaoh, “Hebrew women are stronger{g} than Egyptian women. By the time a midwife arrives, the baby is already born.”
God was good to the midwives, and the people kept growing in number and strength.
Because the midwives honored God, he gave them families of their own.{h}
Then Pharaoh gave a command to his whole nation: “Every boy born to the Hebrews{i} must be drowned in the Nile. Let the girls live.”

notes.text: Some ancient copies, including a Dead Sea Scroll and the Septuagint, say “seventy-five.” That is the number Stephen gives in Acts 7:14.
Or “teemed.” These words remind us of God’s blessing in Genesis 1:28.
Pithom probably means “house of Atum” (an Egyptian god). Rameses was named for the Egyptian kings of that name.
“Pharaoh” is a title that means “great house,” or the royal palace. Exodus never gives this king’s personal name.
Shiphrah probably means “beautiful,” and Puah may mean “splendid.” Both meanings are uncertain.
Hebrew “on the two stones,” most likely a seat or pair of stones a woman used while giving birth.
The Hebrew word is rare. It may mean “lively,” or it may mean they give birth as easily as animals do.
Literally “he made houses for them.”
Some ancient copies, including the Septuagint, add “to the Hebrews.” The Hebrew text leaves it out, but the sense is the same.

verses.text: One man from the house of Levi took a wife from that same tribe.{a}
She conceived and bore a son. Seeing that he was a fine child,{b} she kept him out of sight for three months.
After that she could hide him no longer. So she wove a basket{c} from papyrus, waterproofed it with tar and pitch, laid the baby inside, and left it in the tall reeds beside the Nile.
The baby’s sister stood a little way off to see what would become of him.
Pharaoh’s daughter came down to the river to bathe, and her attendants strolled along the bank. She noticed the basket among the reeds and sent a slave girl to fetch it.
When she lifted the lid, she saw a baby boy, and he was crying. Her heart went out to him. “This is one of the Hebrews’ babies,” she said.
Then the baby’s sister approached her. “Shall I go find a Hebrew woman to nurse him for you?” she asked.
“Please do,” Pharaoh’s daughter said, and the girl ran off to get the child’s mother.
“Take him with you and nurse him,” Pharaoh’s daughter said to the woman. “I will pay your wages.” So the mother took the baby and fed him herself.
As he grew, she took him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became that woman’s son. She gave him the name Moses{d} because, she said, “I drew him up out of the water.”
After Moses was grown, he visited his own people one day and saw how hard they were made to work. There he watched an Egyptian beat a Hebrew, one of his own people.
Moses looked all around, saw nobody, struck the Egyptian dead, and buried him in the sand.
When he went out the following day, two Hebrews were in a fight. “Why do you hit your own countryman?” he asked the man who was at fault.
The man shot back, “Who made you our ruler and judge? Are you planning to kill me the way you killed that Egyptian?” Moses became afraid. “Everybody must know what I did,” he thought.
When Pharaoh learned of this, he looked for a way to kill Moses. But Moses fled from him to the land of Midian,{e} where he stopped at a well.
The priest of Midian had seven daughters. They arrived at the well, drew water, and filled the troughs for the flock their father owned.
Some shepherds came and chased them off, but Moses jumped up, defended the girls, and watered their animals.
When the girls came home to their father Reuel,{f} he asked, “How did you get back so early today?”
“An Egyptian saved us from the shepherds,” they said. “He even drew water for us and watered the flock.”
“So where is he?” Reuel asked. “Why did you leave him there? Go and invite him to a meal.”
Moses agreed to live with Reuel, and Reuel gave him his daughter Zipporah{g} in marriage.
She had a son, and Moses named him Gershom,{h} saying, “I am a foreigner living in a foreign land.”{i}
Years went by, and Egypt’s king died. The Israelites were still moaning in their slavery. They cried for help, and the sound of it climbed up to God.
God heard their groaning and called to mind his covenant promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.{j}
and he looked on the Israelites and understood their need.{k}

notes.text: Her name was Jochebed, and her husband was Amram (see 6:20).
The Hebrew word is “good,” the same word used in Genesis 1 when God saw that his work was good.
The Hebrew word for this basket is used only here and for Noah’s ark.
Moses sounds like a Hebrew word meaning “pull out.” It also resembles an Egyptian word for “child” or “born.”
Midian was a land in northwest Arabia. Its people came from Abraham’s son by Keturah (Genesis 25:2).
Reuel means “friend of God.” He is also called Jethro (3:1).
Zipporah means “bird.”
Gershom sounds like the Hebrew for “a foreigner there.”
Some ancient copies add that Moses had a second son, Eliezer, whose name means “my God is my helper” (see 18:4).
Hebrew “his covenant” with them. A covenant is a binding promise.
Literally “God knew.” Some ancient copies say “God made himself known to them.”

verses.text: Moses was tending the sheep and goats of Jethro,{a} his father-in-law and the priest of Midian. He led them to the far side of the desert and came to Horeb,{b} God’s mountain.
The angel of Yahweh{c} appeared to him as a blazing flame inside a bush.{d} Moses stared. The bush was burning, yet it was not turning to ashes.
“I will go over and look at this amazing sight,” Moses said to himself. “Why doesn’t the bush burn up?”
Yahweh saw Moses step closer for a better look, and God called out from the bush, “Moses! Moses!” Moses answered, “Yes, I am here.”
“Stay back,” God said. “Remove your sandals, for the ground under your feet is holy.”
“I am the God of your father,{e}” he said. “Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob worshiped me.” Afraid to look at God, Moses covered his face.
Yahweh said, “I have indeed seen my people suffer in Egypt, and I have heard how they cry to be freed from their slave drivers. Their pain is known to me.

I have come down to save them from the Egyptians’ power and to bring them out of that land into a good, spacious land, one flowing with milk and honey.{f} It belongs now to the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.{g}
Now the Israelites’ cry has reached me, and I have watched the Egyptians crush them.
Go! I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring my people the Israelites out of Egypt.”
Moses asked God, “Who am I, that Pharaoh should see me and that I should lead the Israelites out of Egypt?”
“I will be with you,{h}” God said. “As proof that I am the one sending you, know this: you will lead the people out of Egypt, and then you will worship me right here on this mountain.”
Moses said, “Suppose I arrive among the Israelites and announce, ‘Your ancestors’ God has sent me.’ They will ask me his name. What should I tell them?”
God said to Moses, “I am who I am.{i} Tell the Israelites this: ‘I am{j} sent me to you.’”

God said more to Moses: “Tell the Israelites that Yahweh{k} sent you, the God of their ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. This is my name for all time, and it is how all generations will call on me.

Now go and assemble Israel’s elders. Tell them that Yahweh, the God their ancestors worshiped, has appeared to you. Say that he told you, ‘I have been watching over you{l} and have seen how Egypt treats you.
I have decided to bring you out of Egypt’s misery and into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey.’

The elders will pay attention to you. After that, you and they will go before the king of Egypt and say, ‘Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Allow us a journey of three days into the desert, where we may sacrifice to Yahweh our God.’
I know, though, that the king of Egypt will refuse to let you leave unless a mighty hand forces him.{m}
So I will reach out and strike Egypt with every wonder I will perform there, and after that he will send you away.
I will also make the Egyptians kind to my people, so you will not leave with empty hands.

Every woman will ask her neighbor, and any foreigner staying in her neighbor’s home, for gold and silver ornaments and for garments. Your sons and daughters will wear them. In this way you will strip the Egyptians of their wealth.”

notes.text: Jethro probably means “abundance.” He is the same man as Reuel (2:18).
Horeb means “dry” or “bare.” It is another name for Mount Sinai.
Yahweh is God’s personal name, written in Hebrew with the four letters YHWH. See the note at verse 15. Verse 4 shows that the angel of Yahweh is Yahweh himself speaking.
This was a thorny bush. The Hebrew word for it sounds like “Sinai.”
Some ancient copies say “fathers,” as in verses 13 and 15.
This means a rich land with good pasture for flocks, and with fruit and bees.
Some ancient copies add the Girgashites, to make a list of seven peoples (see Deuteronomy 7:1).
The Hebrew word for “I will be” prepares us for the name God gives in verse 14.
The Hebrew words can also mean “I will be who I will be.” The name speaks of God’s own life, and of his faithful presence with his people.
Or “I will be.” The Septuagint says “The one who is.”

Yahweh comes from the same Hebrew verb as “I am.” In God’s own mouth the name is “I am,” and when others say it, it is “he is.” Out of respect, Jewish readers long ago stopped saying the name aloud and read “Lord” instead. Many English Bibles print “the LORD.”
Or “I have come to your aid.” Joseph used the same words in Genesis 50:24.
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint says “except by a mighty hand.”

verses.text: “But suppose they do not believe me,” Moses objected. “Suppose they refuse to listen and say, ‘Yahweh never appeared to you.’”
“What is in your hand?” Yahweh asked. “A walking stick,” Moses answered.
“Drop it on the ground,” Yahweh said. When Moses dropped it, it became a snake, and he backed away.
Yahweh told him, “Stretch out your hand and take it by the tail.” Moses reached out and grabbed it, and it was a stick in his hand again.
“That is how they will come to believe,” Yahweh said, “that Yahweh, their ancestors’ God, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, has appeared to you.”
Yahweh gave another command: “Slip your hand inside your robe.” Moses put it in, and when he pulled it out, the skin was covered with a disease{a} and as white as snow.
“Put it back inside,” Yahweh said. Moses did so, and when he drew it out, the hand was as healthy as the rest of him.
Yahweh went on, “If they do not believe you after the first sign, the second sign may convince them.
If even these two signs fail to convince them, scoop some water from the Nile and pour it on dry ground. On the ground the water will turn to blood.”
“Lord,{b} please,” Moses said to Yahweh. “Speaking has never been my gift, not in the past and not since you started talking to me. My mouth and tongue are slow.”
Yahweh said, “Who gave people their mouths? Who makes someone unable to speak or to hear, or gives someone sight or blindness? Is it not I, Yahweh?
“Go,” said Yahweh. “I will help your mouth, and I will teach you your words.”
“Please, Lord,” Moses said, “send somebody else. Anyone at all.”{c}

Then Yahweh’s anger flared against Moses. “Is there not Aaron,{d} your Levite brother?” he asked. “He is a fine speaker, I know. In fact, he is on his way out to meet you now, and seeing you will make him glad.
You will give him the words to say, putting them in his mouth. I will help the two of you speak and will show each of you what to do.
He will be your spokesman to the people, and to him you will stand in the place of God.{e}
With this stick in your hand you will perform the signs.”
Moses returned to the home of his father-in-law, Jethro.{f} “May I return to my relatives in Egypt and see whether any are still alive?” he asked. Jethro said, “Go in peace.”
In Midian, Yahweh told Moses, “Go back to Egypt. Every man who wanted to kill you is dead.”
So Moses put his wife and sons on a donkey and started for Egypt, carrying the stick of God in his hand.

Yahweh said to Moses, “As you go back to Egypt, make sure that you perform before Pharaoh every wonder I have put in your power. Pharaoh’s heart, however, I will make stubborn,{g} and he will refuse to release the people.
Then tell Pharaoh that this is Yahweh’s message: ‘Israel is my own firstborn son.
My command to you was, “Release my son so that he may worship me.” Since you refused, I will now kill your firstborn son.’”
Along the way, at a place where they camped for the night, Yahweh met Moses{h} and was about to kill him.
Then Zipporah took a sharp flint and cut her son’s foreskin off. She touched it to his feet{i} and said, “To me you are a bridegroom of blood!”
So Yahweh left him alone. That was when she said “bridegroom of blood,” speaking of the circumcision.{j}
Yahweh said to Aaron, “Go meet Moses in the desert.” Aaron went, found Moses at the mountain of God, and gave him a kiss.
Moses told Aaron everything Yahweh had said when he sent him, and every sign Yahweh had ordered him to do.
Then Moses and Aaron went and called together all the elders of Israel.
Aaron repeated everything Yahweh had told Moses, and he did the signs as the people watched.
The people believed. They heard that Yahweh had taken notice of the Israelites and had seen their misery, and they bowed down and worshiped.

notes.text: The Hebrew word covers many skin diseases, not only leprosy as we know it today.
Hebrew Adonai, which means “Lord.” It is a respectful title, not God’s name. It is used again in verse 13.
Literally “send by the hand of whomever you will send.”
The meaning of Aaron’s name is not certain. It may be an Egyptian name.
Moses would give Aaron God’s words the way God gives his words to a prophet (see 7:1).
Hebrew has “Jether,” a short form of Jethro. The Samaritan Pentateuch and a few Hebrew copies say “Jethro.”

Hebrew “make strong.” Exodus uses three different verbs for Pharaoh’s hard heart: “make strong,” “make heavy,” and “make hard.” Sometimes God does it, sometimes Pharaoh does, and sometimes the text only says his heart was hard.
The Hebrew says only “met him.” It is not clear if “him” means Moses or his son. The Septuagint says “an angel of the Lord met him.”
The Hebrew says “his feet.” It does not say whose feet they were. This old story is brief, and its details are uncertain.
Zipporah’s act seems to make up for a circumcision that had been skipped, and so to turn away the danger.

verses.text: Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh with this message: “Yahweh, the God of Israel, says, ‘Let my people go so they can hold a festival in my honor in the desert.’”
Pharaoh replied, “Who is Yahweh? Why would I obey him and release Israel? I have never heard of Yahweh, and I will not let Israel go.”
They said, “The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Let us walk three days into the desert and offer sacrifices to Yahweh our God. Otherwise he may strike us with sickness or the sword.”
Egypt’s king told them, “Moses and Aaron, why do you draw these people away from their work? Get back to your jobs!”
“There are so many of them now,” he said, “and you want them to rest!”
On that very day Pharaoh gave this order to the people’s slave drivers and to the Israelite foremen:{a}
“No longer supply the people with straw for their bricks. They must go out and collect it on their own,
but the daily brick count must stay as high as before. Do not lower the quota. They are lazy, and that explains why they plead, ‘We must go and make sacrifices to our God!’
Pile more work on the men and keep them busy, so they will not listen to lies.”
The slave drivers and foremen went out to the people with this message: “Pharaoh says, ‘I will not give you straw.
Find it yourselves, wherever you can, but you will make just as many bricks as before.’”
So the people scattered all across Egypt to collect stubble in place of straw.
The slave drivers pushed them constantly. “Finish your daily number of bricks,” they said, “just as you did when you had straw.”
The Israelite foremen, who had been appointed by Pharaoh’s slave drivers, were beaten and asked, “Why didn’t you make the full number of bricks yesterday or today, as you did before?”
The Israelite foremen then went to Pharaoh and pleaded, “Why are you treating your servants like this?
No straw is handed to your servants, but we hear, ‘Make bricks!’ We are the ones beaten, though the fault lies with your own people.”{b}
“You are lazy!” Pharaoh answered. “Lazy! That is why you keep saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to Yahweh.’
Get back to work. You will get no straw, but you must still hand in the full number of bricks.”
The Israelite foremen realized they were in serious trouble when they heard, “You must not make fewer bricks each day.”
Moses and Aaron were standing in their path as the foremen came away from Pharaoh.
“May Yahweh see what you have done and judge you,” they said. “You have made us hateful to Pharaoh and his officials. You have handed them a sword to kill us.”
Moses went back to Yahweh and said, “Lord,{c} why have you made things worse for these people? Why did you send me at all?
From the moment I went to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has made things worse for these people, and you have not rescued them at all.”

notes.text: These were Israelite officials, set over their own people by the Egyptian slave drivers (see verse 14).
The Hebrew is hard to understand. It says literally “and your people sin.” The Septuagint says “you wrong your people.”
Hebrew Adonai, “Lord.”

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses, “Now you will watch what I do to Pharaoh. Forced by a strong hand, he will let them go. Forced by a strong hand, he will drive them out of his land.”
God spoke to Moses again. “I am Yahweh,” he said.
“Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob knew me as El Shaddai,{a} but they were not told my name, Yahweh.{b}
I also made a promise{c} to them to give them Canaan, the land where they lived as outsiders.
Now I have heard the Israelites groaning under the Egyptians who enslave them, and I have remembered my promise.
Tell the Israelites this: ‘I am Yahweh. I will lift the Egyptians’ heavy loads from you and set you free from slavery. I will redeem{d} you with my arm stretched out and with great acts of judgment.
I will take you for my own people and be your God. Then you will realize that I, Yahweh your God, am the one who freed you from the Egyptians’ heavy loads.
The land that I swore{e} to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is where I will take you, and I will hand it over to you as your own possession. I am Yahweh.’”
Moses gave the Israelites this message, but they paid no attention. Discouragement{f} and brutal slavery had worn them down.
Then Yahweh said to Moses,
“Go in and order Pharaoh, Egypt’s king, to release the Israelites from his country.”
“The Israelites would not even hear me,” Moses said to Yahweh. “How will Pharaoh hear me? I am a poor speaker.”{g}
Yahweh now gave Moses and Aaron their orders about the Israelites and about Pharaoh, king of Egypt. They were to lead Israel out of the country.
These were the heads of their family groups. Reuben, Israel’s oldest son, had sons named Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. Those are the clans of Reuben.
Simeon’s sons were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, whose mother was a Canaanite. Those are the clans of Simeon.
Levi’s sons, in the order of their birth, were Gershon,{h} Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years.
Gershon’s sons, by clan, were Libni and Shimei.
Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel were the sons of Kohath, who lived 133 years.
Merari’s sons were Mahli and Mushi. These are the Levite clans by their birth order.
Amram took his father’s sister Jochebed{i} as his wife, and their children were Aaron and Moses.{j} Amram’s life lasted 137 years.{k}
Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri were the sons of Izhar.
Uzziel had sons named Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
Elisheba{l} became Aaron’s wife. She was Amminadab’s daughter and Nahshon’s sister, and the children she bore him were Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar,{m} and Ithamar.
Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph were the three sons of Korah, and they are the Korahite clans.
Aaron’s son Eleazar married a daughter of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas.{n} These are the heads of the Levite family groups, by clan.
These are the very same Aaron and Moses whom Yahweh told, “Bring the Israelites out of Egypt, division by division.”{o}
They were the men who spoke to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to demand that he release the Israelites. It was this same Moses and Aaron.
On the day Yahweh spoke to Moses in Egypt,
“I am Yahweh,” he said. “Take to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, every word I give you.”
Moses said to Yahweh, “I speak poorly. How can I expect Pharaoh to listen?”

notes.text: El Shaddai is often translated “God Almighty.” Its exact meaning is uncertain. It may mean “God of the mountain” or “the God who is enough.” God used this name with Abraham in Genesis 17:1.

Or as a question: “Did I not tell them my name, Yahweh?” The name is used often in Genesis, so the point is probably that the fathers had not yet seen all that the name means: a God who keeps his promises by rescuing his people.
Hebrew “covenant,” a binding promise.
Redeem means to buy back a relative from slavery, as a family member would do.
Literally “I lifted my hand,” which was a way of making an oath.
Hebrew “shortness of spirit,” meaning they were discouraged or had no patience left.
Hebrew “I am uncircumcised of lips,” which means his lips were not ready for speaking. Compare 4:10.
Gershon is a different person from Moses’ son Gershom (2:22).
Jochebed probably means “Yahweh is glory.” The Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate say Jochebed was Amram’s cousin instead of his aunt.
The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint add “and their sister Miriam.”
The Septuagint has a different number, 132 or 136 in some copies.
Elisheba probably means “my God has promised.” It is the same name as Elizabeth in the New Testament.
Eleazar means “God has helped.”
Phinehas is an Egyptian name that probably means “the Nubian.”
The Hebrew word means “armies.” Israel left Egypt in order, like an army.

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses, “I am making you like God{a} to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your spokesman.
You will say all that I order you to say, and Aaron will tell Pharaoh to send the Israelites away from his land.
I will make Pharaoh stubborn,{b} though, and I will pile up my signs and wonders in Egypt.
Pharaoh will not obey you. Then I will bring my hand down on Egypt and lead out my armies, the people of Israel, with terrible judgments.
When I reach out my hand against Egypt and bring the Israelites away from it, the Egyptians will know that I am Yahweh.”
Moses and Aaron obeyed Yahweh to the letter.
At the time of their talks with Pharaoh, Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three.
Yahweh said to Moses and Aaron,
“If Pharaoh says to you, ‘Prove yourselves with a wonder,’ have Aaron throw his stick down in front of him, and it will change into a large snake.”{c}
Moses and Aaron entered Pharaoh’s court and did what Yahweh had commanded. There, with Pharaoh and his officials watching, Aaron threw down the stick, and it became a snake.
Pharaoh summoned his own wise men and sorcerers, and the magicians{d} of Egypt used their secret arts to do the same thing.
Every one of them threw down a stick, and every stick became a snake. Aaron’s stick, however, swallowed theirs.
Still, Pharaoh’s heart stayed hard. He would not listen to them, as Yahweh had said he would not.
Yahweh told Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart is stubborn,{e} and he refuses to free the people.
Meet him in the morning, when he walks out to the water. Wait for him on the bank of the Nile, with the stick that turned into a snake in your hand.
Tell him, ‘Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you. His order is this: “Free my people, and they will serve me in the desert.” So far you have not obeyed.
So Yahweh says, “Here is how you will learn that I am Yahweh: with the stick in my hand I will strike the Nile, and its water will become blood.
The Nile’s fish will die, the water will smell foul, and the Egyptians will be unable to drink from the river.”’”{f}

Yahweh told Moses, “Have Aaron take his stick and stretch his hand over every water source in Egypt: rivers, canals, ponds, and every pool. All of it will become blood. Throughout Egypt there will be blood, even in wooden buckets and stone jars.”
Moses and Aaron obeyed Yahweh. Aaron lifted the stick and struck the Nile while Pharaoh and his officials watched, and all the river water turned to blood.
The fish in the Nile died, and the river smelled so bad that the Egyptians could not drink from it. Blood covered the whole land of Egypt.
The magicians of Egypt, however, used their secret arts to do the same. Pharaoh’s heart stayed hard, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron, as Yahweh had said.
Pharaoh turned around and walked into his palace. Not even this made him think.
All the Egyptians dug along the Nile for drinking water, because the river water was undrinkable.
A full week went by after Yahweh struck the Nile.

notes.text: The Hebrew word is “God” (or “a god”). Moses would speak with God’s authority, and Aaron would speak for him as a prophet speaks for God (see 4:16).
Hebrew “make hard.” See the note at 4:21.
This Hebrew word is different from the one for “snake” in 4:3. It can mean a big serpent or a sea creature such as a crocodile.
The Hebrew word comes from Egyptian. It means priests who knew sacred writings and magic. Jewish tradition names two of them, Jannes and Jambres (2 Timothy 3:8).
Hebrew “heavy.” See the note at 4:21.

In the plague stories (chapters 7 to 11), the Samaritan Pentateuch and a Dead Sea Scroll add passages that repeat God’s words as Moses and Aaron carry them out. This translation follows the shorter Hebrew text.

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses,{a} “Go to Pharaoh and give him this message: ‘This is what Yahweh says: Set my people free, and they will worship me.
If you refuse, I will plague your whole country with frogs.

The Nile will teem with them. They will crawl into your palace, your bedroom, and even onto your bed. They will get into your officials’ houses, into your people’s homes, into your ovens, and into your bowls for kneading dough.
Frogs will leap onto you, your people, and all your officials.’”
Yahweh told Moses, “Tell Aaron to hold his stick over the rivers, canals, and ponds and make frogs come up all over Egypt.”
Aaron held out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs{b} came up and covered the land.
The magicians used their secret arts to do the same, and they too made frogs come up over Egypt.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. “Ask Yahweh to remove the frogs from me and from my people,” he said. “Then I will release your people to offer sacrifices to Yahweh.”

“You may decide when,{c}” Moses said. “At what time should I pray for you, for your officials, and for your people, so that the frogs are taken away from you and your homes and stay only in the Nile?”
“Tomorrow,” said Pharaoh. “It will be as you say,” Moses replied, “so that you may know no one compares to Yahweh our God.
Your officials, your people, and your houses will all be free of frogs. Only the Nile will keep them.”
Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh, and Moses begged Yahweh about the frogs he had sent against Pharaoh.
Yahweh carried out Moses’ request. Frogs lay dead throughout the houses, courtyards, and fields.
The Egyptians piled them into heaps, and the land reeked.
But when Pharaoh saw that the trouble was over, he made his heart stubborn again and would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as Yahweh had said.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell Aaron to strike the soil with his stick, and across all Egypt the dust will become gnats.”{d}
They did it. Aaron held out his hand with the stick and struck the dust, and gnats landed on people and animals. All the dust in Egypt turned to gnats.
The magicians tried to make gnats with their secret arts, but they could not. Gnats covered people and animals.
The magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God.” Still, Pharaoh’s heart stayed hard, and he refused to listen to them, as Yahweh had predicted.
Yahweh told Moses, “Rise early and stand where Pharaoh will pass as he goes down to the water. Tell him, ‘Yahweh says: Send my people out so they may serve me.
Otherwise swarms of flies{e} will come from me against Pharaoh, his officials, his people, and all their houses. Egyptian homes will fill with flies, and even the ground will be black with them.
That day, though, I will set apart Goshen, where my people live. No swarm will enter it, and you will know that I, Yahweh, am present in this land.{f}
I will set my people apart{g} from your people. This sign will happen tomorrow.’”
Yahweh did it. Thick swarms of flies poured into Pharaoh’s palace and into his officials’ houses, and the whole country was ruined by them.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. “Offer your sacrifices to your God,” he said, “but you must stay in this country to do it.”
“That would not be right,” Moses said. “The Egyptians find the sacrifices we make to Yahweh our God disgusting. If they saw us make those sacrifices, would they not stone us?
We need to make a three-day trip into the desert to sacrifice to Yahweh our God, just as he has told us.”
Pharaoh answered, “You may sacrifice to Yahweh your God in the desert, but you cannot travel far. And ask Yahweh to help me too.”

“Once I have left your presence,” Moses said, “I will ask Yahweh, and tomorrow the flies will go away from Pharaoh, his officials, and his people. But Pharaoh must stop playing tricks and release the people to sacrifice to Yahweh.”
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to Yahweh.
Yahweh granted Moses’ request, and every fly went away from the king, his officials, and his people. None were left.
Yet this time too Pharaoh made his heart stubborn, and he did not let the people go.

notes.text: In the Hebrew text, 8:1-4 are numbered 7:26-29, and 8:5-32 are numbered 8:1-28.
The Hebrew says “the frog,” which means frogs in general.
Literally “have the glory over me,” a polite way of letting Pharaoh pick the time.
Or “lice.” The exact insect is uncertain.
Hebrew “swarm” or “mixture.” The Septuagint says “dog flies.” Some Jewish teachers thought it meant a mixture of wild animals.
Or “I, Yahweh, am in the middle of the land.”
So the Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate. The Hebrew says “redemption,” which may be a copying mistake for “separation.”

verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Go before Pharaoh and give him this word from Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews: ‘Send my people away so that they may worship me.
If you still refuse to release them and keep holding them back,
the hand of Yahweh will strike your animals in the fields with a terrible disease. It will hit the horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, sheep, and goats.
But Yahweh will treat Israel’s animals differently from Egypt’s, and nothing that belongs to the Israelites will die.’”
Yahweh fixed the time. “Tomorrow,” he said, “Yahweh will carry this out in the land.”
The following day Yahweh did it. Egypt’s animals died,{a} yet of the Israelites’ animals not one was lost.
Pharaoh sent men to check and learned that none of Israel’s animals had died. Even so, his heart stayed stubborn, and he did not release the people.
Yahweh told Moses and Aaron, “Take two fistfuls of furnace ash. Moses is to throw it toward the sky as Pharaoh watches.
They will turn into fine dust that spreads over the whole land of Egypt, and it will make painful sores break out on people and animals everywhere in Egypt.”
They took ashes from the furnace and presented themselves to Pharaoh. Moses flung them skyward, and festering sores appeared on people and on animals.
The magicians could not even stand in front of Moses, because they, like all the Egyptians, were covered with sores.
But Yahweh made Pharaoh’s heart hard, and he would not listen to Moses and Aaron, exactly as Yahweh had told Moses.
Yahweh told Moses, “Rise early in the morning, go before Pharaoh, and give him this word: ‘Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, says, Allow my people to leave and worship me.
This time I am sending every one of my plagues at you,{b} at your officials, and at your people. Then you will learn that there is nobody like me anywhere on earth.
I could have reached out my hand already and wiped you and your people off the earth with a disease.
Yet I have let you remain{c} for a purpose. By you I will display my power, and my name will be proclaimed across the whole earth.
You continue to stand in the way of my people and will not let them leave.
At this time tomorrow I will send down the heaviest hail Egypt has seen since the day it became a nation.
Order your animals and everything you have in the open to be brought under cover. Every person or animal still outside when the hail falls will die.’”
Those among Pharaoh’s officials who respected Yahweh’s word hurried their servants and animals indoors.
Those who ignored Yahweh’s word left their servants and animals out in the fields.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Hold your hand up toward the sky. Hail will fall on all of Egypt, on people, on animals, and on every plant in the fields.”
Moses held his stick toward the sky, and Yahweh sent thunder{d} and hail, with lightning striking the ground. Yahweh rained hail down on Egypt.
Hail fell, and lightning flashed through it without a break. It was the worst storm in the whole history of Egypt as a nation.
Across Egypt the hail beat down everything in the open, people and animals alike. It flattened every plant in the fields and splintered every tree.
Goshen, where the Israelites lived, was the one place that had no hail.
Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron in. “I have sinned this time,” he said. “Yahweh is the righteous one. My people and I are the guilty ones.
Ask Yahweh to stop this thunder{e} and hail, because it is more than we can bear. I will let you leave; you need not stay here a moment longer.”
“As soon as I am out of the city,” Moses told him, “I will spread my hands toward Yahweh. The thunder will cease and the hail will end, and you will see that the earth belongs to Yahweh.
But you and your officials, I know, do not yet fear Yahweh God.”{f}
(The flax and barley were ruined, since barley had its heads formed and flax was in bloom.
The wheat and spelt{g} were not ruined, since they come up later.)
Moses walked out of the city, away from Pharaoh, and spread his hands toward Yahweh. The thunder and the hail ceased, and the downpour ended.
When the downpour, the hail, and the thunder were over, Pharaoh saw it and went on sinning. He and his officials hardened their hearts.
Pharaoh’s heart stayed hard, and he did not release the Israelites, just as Yahweh had said through Moses.

notes.text: This means all the animals that were out in the fields (verse 3). Animals show up again in verses 19 to 25, probably ones that had been kept indoors or were bought later.
Or “against you yourself.” It may mean the plagues would be aimed at Pharaoh’s own will.
Or “I have raised you up.” Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9:17.
Hebrew “voices,” a common way of saying thunder. The same word is used in verses 28, 29, 33, and 34.
Hebrew “voices of God,” or “mighty thunder.”
The title “Yahweh God” is rare in the first five books outside Genesis 2 and 3. The Septuagint says “the Lord.”
Or “emmer,” an old kind of wheat.

verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh. His heart, and the hearts of his officials, I have made stubborn, so that I can show these signs of mine among them.
You will also be able to tell your children and grandchildren how harshly I dealt with Egypt and about the signs I showed there. That is how you will all know that I am Yahweh.”
Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh with this message: “Yahweh, the God of the Hebrews, asks, ‘How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Release my people to serve me.
Refuse, and tomorrow I will bring locusts into your land.
They will cover the ground until nobody can see it. They will eat what the hail left you, and they will strip every tree growing in your fields.

They will fill your houses, the houses of your officials, and the houses of every Egyptian. Neither your parents nor your grandparents ever saw such a thing since they were born.’” Then Moses turned and left Pharaoh.
Pharaoh’s officials protested, “How long is this man going to be a snare for us? Let the men go and worship Yahweh their God. Can you not see that Egypt is ruined?”
Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. “Go and worship Yahweh your God,” he said. “But exactly who will be going?”
“All of us will go,” Moses said, “young and old. Our sons and daughters will go, and so will our sheep, goats, and cattle, since we have a festival of Yahweh to observe.”
Pharaoh said, “Yahweh will be with you, all right, if I ever let your little ones go with you!{a} Look, you are plotting something evil.
Not at all! Just the men may go and worship Yahweh, since that is what you were asking.” Then Moses and Aaron were driven away from Pharaoh.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Hold your hand out over Egypt to bring the locusts. They will swarm over the land and eat every plant the hail left.”
Moses held out his stick over Egypt, and Yahweh drove an east wind across the land through that whole day and night. By dawn the wind had brought the locusts in.
The locusts flew over all Egypt and landed throughout the country in swarms so thick that nothing like them had come before or ever will again.

They hid the ground until the land turned dark. Every plant was eaten, and so was all the fruit on the trees that the hail had spared. Nothing green was left in the whole land of Egypt, on tree or in field.
Pharaoh quickly called for Moses and Aaron. “I have sinned against Yahweh your God and against you,” he said.
Forgive my sin one more time, I beg you. Ask Yahweh your God to take this deadly thing away from me.”
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to Yahweh.
Then Yahweh turned the wind around. A very powerful west wind{b} lifted the locusts and swept them into the Red Sea,{c} until not one was left in all the land of Egypt.
Yahweh, however, made Pharaoh stubborn, and he would not release the Israelites.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Hold your hand up toward the sky, and darkness will cover Egypt, a darkness so thick it can be felt.”
Moses held his hand up toward the sky, and total darkness settled over Egypt for three days.
Nobody could see anyone else, and nobody left his place for three days. Where the Israelites lived, though, there was light.
Again Pharaoh summoned Moses. “Go and worship Yahweh,” he said. “Leave your sheep, goats, and cattle here. Your children may go with you.”
“No,” said Moses. “You will have to supply sacrifices and burnt offerings for us to give to Yahweh our God.
Our animals must go with us. Not a hoof can stay behind, because we will use some of them to worship Yahweh our God, and we will not know which ones until we get there.”
But Yahweh made Pharaoh’s heart hard, and he refused to let them go.
“Get out of my sight!” Pharaoh told him. “Make sure you never see my face again. The day you do, you will die.”
“You have spoken well,” Moses said. “I will never see your face again.”

notes.text: Pharaoh is being sarcastic. He means “Yahweh will be with you only if I let your children go, and I never will.”
Hebrew “a sea wind,” meaning a wind from the Mediterranean Sea to the west of Egypt.
Hebrew “Sea of Reeds.” The same name is used in the Bible for the Gulf of Suez, the Gulf of Aqaba, and perhaps marshy lakes near the Isthmus of Suez. Where Israel crossed (chapter 14) is uncertain.

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses, “One more blow is coming for Pharaoh and Egypt. After it, Pharaoh will let you leave. In fact, he will push all of you out of the country.
Now speak to the people. Every man and every woman should ask the neighbors next door for things made of silver and gold.”
Yahweh made the Egyptians kind toward his people. Moses himself had also become a highly respected man in Egypt, admired by Pharaoh’s officials and by the Egyptian people.
Moses announced to Pharaoh, “Yahweh says: ‘Around midnight{a} I will pass through the middle of Egypt.
Every oldest son in Egypt will die. That includes the son of Pharaoh who sits on the throne and the son of the slave woman who grinds grain. Even the first young of every farm animal will die.
Such a wail of grief will rise over Egypt as has never been heard before and will never be heard again.
But among the Israelites, not even a dog will bark at a person or an animal.{b} Then you will know that Yahweh makes a difference between Egypt and Israel.’
All these officials of yours will come to me, kneel at my feet, and say, ‘Leave, you and everyone who follows you.’ Only then will I go.” Moses then walked away from Pharaoh, burning with anger.
Yahweh had warned Moses, “Pharaoh will refuse to listen to you. That is how I will be able to do even more wonders in Egypt.”
Before Pharaoh, Moses and Aaron carried out every one of these wonders. Still, Yahweh kept Pharaoh’s heart stubborn, so Pharaoh did not let the Israelites leave his land.

notes.text: Hebrew “about the middle of the night.” Midnight is the middle of the night, the time when Yahweh will act.
Hebrew “no dog will sharpen its tongue.” This was a way of saying that not even a dog would make a sound.

verses.text: In the land of Egypt, Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron.
He said, “This month will be the beginning of all your months. Count it as month one of your year.{a}
Announce to all the people of Israel: On the tenth day of this month (March–April), every family must choose a lamb.{b} Each household needs one.
If a household is too small to finish a whole lamb, it should join the nearest neighbor. Count the people and share the animal, so that everyone gets as much as he or she can eat.
The animal must have no flaw. It must be a male, one year old, and you may pick either a sheep or a goat.
Keep it safe until the fourteenth day of the month (March–April). At twilight{c} that day, every family in Israel will kill its animal.
Catch some of the blood and put it on the two side posts and the top beam of the doorway in each house where the meal is eaten.
The meat must be eaten that same night, roasted over a fire, together with bitter herbs and bread made without yeast.{d}
Never eat any of it raw, and never boil it in water. Roast the whole animal, head, legs, and insides together.
Leave nothing for the morning. If any meat is left by then, burn it.
Eat it dressed for travel, with your belt tied, your sandals on, and your walking stick in hand. Eat in a hurry. This is Yahweh’s Passover.{e}
Tonight I will go through Egypt and strike down the oldest son of every family and the first young of every animal. I will also judge every god of Egypt. I am Yahweh.
The blood on your houses will mark where you live. When I see it, I will pass over you. The disaster I bring on Egypt will not touch you.
“Remember this day. Celebrate it every year as a feast for Yahweh. It is a rule for all time, for you and for your descendants.
For seven days your bread must have no yeast. Clear every bit of yeast out of your houses on the first day. Whoever eats yeast bread at any time from day one to day seven will be removed from Israel.
Hold a holy gathering on the first day and another on the seventh. Do no work on those days, except preparing the food everyone needs.
Keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, since this is the very day I marched your tribes out of Egypt. Honor this day in every generation by a law that never expires.
Starting at sundown on the fourteenth day of the first month (March–April),{f} eat bread without yeast, and keep eating it until sundown on the twenty-first.
For those seven days, your homes must hold no yeast at all. If anyone eats something made with yeast, whether a foreigner or one born in Israel, that person will be removed from the community.
Eat nothing made with yeast. Wherever you live, eat bread without it.”
Moses called all of Israel’s elders together and told them, “Go now and choose a lamb for each of your families, and kill it for the Passover.
Gather a bunch of hyssop,{g} soak it in the blood in the basin, and brush blood on the top beam and the two side posts. Then stay inside your house until it is morning.

Yahweh is about to pass through Egypt and strike the Egyptians down. If he sees blood on the top beam and the side posts, he will skip that door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your homes and hurt you.
Keep this as a rule for yourselves and your children for all time.
When you enter the land Yahweh has promised to give you, keep doing this ceremony.
When your children ask, ‘Why do we do this?’
say this: ‘It is Yahweh’s Passover offering. He skipped over the Israelite houses in Egypt while he struck the Egyptians, and our families were spared.’” The people bowed low and worshiped.
Then the Israelites left and carried it out, doing everything just as Yahweh had commanded Moses and Aaron.

At midnight Yahweh struck down every oldest son in Egypt. That began with Pharaoh’s son, who was to sit on the throne, and reached to the son of the prisoner in the jail.{h} The first young of the animals died as well.
Pharaoh got up that night, and so did all his officials and all the Egyptians. Loud crying filled Egypt, because there was not one house without a death.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron while it was still dark. “Rise and leave my people,” he ordered, “you and the Israelites together. Go worship Yahweh, as you have said you would.
Take your sheep and cattle, as you said, and go. And ask a blessing for me too.”
The Egyptians pressed the people to leave the country quickly. “Otherwise we will all be dead,” they said.
So the people took their dough before the yeast had worked in it. They tied their kneading troughs up in cloth, and each person balanced his on a shoulder.
The Israelites had followed Moses’ instructions and requested silver, gold, and clothing from the Egyptians.
Yahweh had made the Egyptians so kind to the people that they gave whatever was asked. In this way the Israelites took the wealth of Egypt.
The Israelites left Rameses and walked to Succoth.{i} The men alone numbered about 600,000, and the children were counted separately.{j}
A large crowd of other people{k} went with them, together with very many sheep, goats, and cattle.

With the dough they had carried out of Egypt they made round flat loaves without yeast. It had not risen, because the Egyptians had forced them out in such a rush that they could not wait and had packed no other food.
Israel’s time in Egypt added up to 430 years.{l}
On the very last day of those 430 years, all of Yahweh’s tribes left Egypt.
That was a night when Yahweh stayed awake to lead them out of Egypt. So each year on this same night, all Israelites stay awake in honor of Yahweh.
Then Yahweh gave Moses and Aaron the law of the Passover: “No outsider may share in the meal.
A slave that someone has bought may eat it, once he has been circumcised.
A visitor or a hired worker may not eat it.
Eat it in a single house. Take none of the meat outdoors, and break none of its bones.{m}
All the community of Israel must keep this feast.

If a foreigner who lives with you wants to keep Yahweh’s Passover, every male in his household must first be circumcised. Then he may join in and be treated like one born in the land. No man who is uncircumcised may eat it.
The same law applies to a native Israelite and to a foreigner living among you.”
All the Israelites did exactly what Yahweh had told Moses and Aaron.
On that very day Yahweh brought the Israelites out of Egypt, group by group.

notes.text: Hebrew “the first month of the year.” Later it was called Nisan, and an earlier name was Abib (13:4). The Hebrew months followed the moon, so this month covered parts of March and April, and the dates changed a little each year.
Hebrew seh, a young animal of the flock. It could be a lamb or a young goat (verse 5).
Hebrew “between the two evenings.” It may mean the time between sunset and dark, or from mid-afternoon to sunset.
Hebrew matsot, flat bread made without yeast.
Hebrew pesah. The name is linked to the Hebrew verb pasah, which means “to pass over” (verses 13, 23, 27) and may also mean “to protect.”
Hebrew “in the first month.” See the note at verse 2.
Hyssop is probably the plant now called Syrian marjoram. Its small hairy branches soak up liquid well.
Hebrew “the house of the pit,” a dungeon or underground jail.
Rameses was an Egyptian city. Succoth means “shelters” or “huts.”
Hebrew “600,000 men on foot.” The Hebrew word for “thousand” can also mean a family group or military unit, so some readers take the numbers differently.
Hebrew erev rav, “a mixed crowd,” people of other nations who joined Israel.

The Samaritan Pentateuch says “in the land of Canaan and in the land of Egypt,” and the Septuagint is similar. Those copies count the 430 years from Abraham’s arrival in Canaan, as Paul does in Galatians 3:17.
John 19:36 applies this verse to Jesus.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses.
“Set aside for me every firstborn male among the Israelites. The first one born in each family, and the first male of each animal, belongs to me.”
Moses said to the people, “Never forget this day, when you walked out of Egypt, the place where you were slaves. Yahweh’s strong hand brought you out. Eat nothing made with yeast.
You are setting out today. It is the month of Abib (March–April).{a}

Yahweh swore to your ancestors that he would give you a rich land, flowing with milk and honey. It belongs now to the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites. After he brings you in, keep this ceremony every year in this same month.
Eat bread without yeast for seven days. Then on the seventh day, hold a feast for Yahweh.
During those seven days eat only bread without yeast. No bread with yeast and no yeast at all should be seen anywhere in your land.
On that day explain to your child, ‘I do this because of what Yahweh did for me as I was leaving Egypt.’
The feast will serve you like a sign tied on your hand and a memory-aid between your eyes.{b} It will keep Yahweh’s teaching in your mouth, for Yahweh’s strong hand took you out of Egypt.
So keep this rule at its proper time, year after year.
“Yahweh will bring you into Canaan, as he promised you and your ancestors, and he will give you the land.
When that happens, hand over to Yahweh the first child born to every mother, and the first male young of every animal. These males belong to Yahweh.
If you want to keep a firstborn donkey, pay for it with a lamb. If you refuse to pay, you must break its neck. Every firstborn son in your family must be bought back too.
Someday your son will wonder, ‘What is the meaning of this?’ Tell him, ‘Yahweh used his mighty hand to rescue us from Egypt, the land where we were slaves.

Pharaoh stubbornly refused to release us, so Yahweh put to death every firstborn in Egypt, from people down to animals. That is the reason I give Yahweh every firstborn male animal and buy back each of my sons who was born first.’
Wear this like a sign on your hand and a headband{c} on your forehead, since Yahweh brought us out of Egypt with his strong hand.”

When Pharaoh released the people, God avoided the road that runs through Philistine territory, though it was the nearest. He reasoned, “If they see fighting, they may lose heart and turn back toward Egypt.”
Instead God made them take the long way, by the desert road that leads to the Red Sea.{d} When they left Egypt, the Israelites were lined up like an army.

Moses took Joseph’s bones with him. Long ago Joseph had made the Israelites swear a promise. “Certainly God will visit you,” he had told them. “Then you must bring my bones up out of here and take them with you.”{e}
The people left Succoth and camped at Etham, at the edge of the desert.
Yahweh traveled in front of them. In the daytime he guided them as a tall pillar of cloud, and at night he lit their way as a pillar of fire. In this way they were able to march by day and by night.
The column of cloud never left its place in front of the people by day, and the column of fire never left by night.

notes.text: Abib means “ears of grain.” It was the month when the barley was ripe. Later it was called Nisan (see 12:2). It fell in March–April.
Later Jewish practice took this literally and wore small boxes holding Scripture verses, called tefillin. The words may also be a way of saying “keep this always in mind.”
Hebrew totafot, a band or ornament worn on the forehead.
Or “Sea of Reeds.” The Hebrew is yam suf. The Septuagint says “Red Sea,” and the exact body of water is not certain.
Genesis 50:25.

verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses,
“Tell the Israelites to change direction and camp at Pi-hahiroth,{a} which lies between Migdol and the sea. Set up your tents beside the water, facing Baal-zephon.
Pharaoh will say about the Israelites, ‘They are wandering around lost. The desert has closed them in.’

I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and he will chase you. By defeating him and all his army I will win honor for myself,{b} and Egypt will learn that I am Yahweh.” The Israelites followed these instructions.

Word came to the king of Egypt that the people had escaped. At once Pharaoh and his officials felt differently about them. “What did we just do?” they said. “We let Israel go free, and we lost our slave labor!”
Pharaoh got his chariot ready and took his army along.
He selected six hundred of his finest chariots, along with every other chariot in Egypt, and put officers{c} in charge of each one.
Yahweh made the king of Egypt, Pharaoh, stubborn, and Pharaoh chased the Israelites, who were marching out with bold confidence.{d}

The Egyptians went after them with all the horses and chariots of Pharaoh, his horsemen, and his army. As Pharaoh drew near, they found the Israelites camped by the sea, next to Pi-hahiroth and facing Baal-zephon.
As Pharaoh got close, the Israelites looked up and saw the Egyptians marching toward them. They were terrified and cried out to Yahweh.
They said to Moses, “Was Egypt so short of burial places that you had to bring us to the desert to die? Why did you do this to us? Why take us out of Egypt?
In Egypt we told you, ‘Leave us alone and let us work for the Egyptians.’ Slavery in Egypt would be better for us than death in the desert!”
Moses answered the people, “Have no fear. Stay where you are, and you will see Yahweh rescue you today. The Egyptians who are here now, you will never see again.
Yahweh will fight for you. You only need to keep still.”
Yahweh said to Moses, “Why are you crying out to me? Tell the Israelites to move forward.
Raise your stick and reach your hand over the sea, and the sea will divide. Then the Israelites can cross on dry land.
I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so they march in after the Israelites. By defeating Pharaoh, his army, his chariots, and his horsemen, I will win honor for myself.
Once I have been honored through the defeat of Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen, the Egyptians will learn that I am Yahweh.”
Until then the angel of God had gone ahead of Israel’s camp. He now shifted to the back and followed them. The cloud shifted too, leaving the front and settling behind.
So the cloud came to rest between the Egyptian camp and the Israelite camp. It made the Egyptians’ side dark, while it gave light to the Israelites’ side,{e} and the two camps stayed apart all night.
Then Moses lifted his arm above the sea. Yahweh sent a powerful wind from the east that blew all night long. It drove the sea back and left dry ground, and the water divided.
Across the sea bed the Israelites walked, on dry ground. The water stood up like a wall to the right of them and to the left.
The Egyptians went after them. All of Pharaoh’s horses, chariots, and horsemen rushed into the sea behind them.
Yahweh looked down on the Egyptian army from the fiery cloud sometime between two and six in the morning,{f} and he made them panic.
Their chariot wheels came off,{g} and driving became a struggle. “Run away from Israel!” cried the Egyptians. “Yahweh fights for them, and against us!”
Yahweh then said to Moses, “Hold your hand out over the sea so that the water flows back onto the Egyptians, with their chariots and horsemen.”
Moses held out his hand. As day broke, the sea returned to its usual place. The Egyptians ran straight at it, and Yahweh tossed them into the middle of the waves.
The water flowed back and buried every chariot and horseman. Not one man out of Pharaoh’s whole army that had entered the sea was left alive.
But the Israelites had crossed over on dry land, and the sea had formed walls on both sides of them.
On that day Yahweh delivered Israel from Egypt’s power. The Israelites could see Egyptian bodies washed up along the shore.
When they saw the great power Yahweh had used against Egypt, the people respected Yahweh and trusted him and his servant Moses.

notes.text: Pi-hahiroth may be an Egyptian name meaning “house of Hathor” or a Hebrew name meaning “mouth of the canals.” Migdol means “tower.” Baal-zephon means “lord of the north,” the name of a Canaanite god used as a place name. No one knows exactly where these places were.
Hebrew kavod, “glory” or “honor.” The same idea appears in verses 17 and 18.
Hebrew shalishim, perhaps “third men,” that is, the third man in a chariot, or high officers in general.
Hebrew “with a raised hand,” meaning boldly and openly.
The Hebrew is hard to understand. It may mean the cloud was dark for the Egyptians and bright for Israel. The Septuagint says “there was darkness and gloom, and the night passed.”
Hebrew “the morning watch,” the last of the three night watches, from about 2 a.m. to 6 a.m.
Hebrew “he removed the wheels.” The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Syriac say “he bound” or “jammed” them, a difference of one letter.

verses.text:
Moses and the Israelites lifted their voices in a song for Yahweh:
“Yahweh has triumphed gloriously,{a} so I sing to him!
Rider and horse alike{b} he flung into the waves.

Yah{c} is my strength, and he is why I sing,{d}
for he has become my rescuer.
This one is my God, and I give him praise.
My father worshiped him, and I will honor his name.

Yahweh is a fighter.
Yahweh is the name he carries.

Pharaoh’s chariots and his army he dumped into the sea.
The pick of his officers sank beneath the Red Sea.

The deep waters closed over them.
They dropped to the bottom like a rock.

Your right hand, Yahweh, is glorious and strong.
Your right hand, Yahweh, crushed the enemy.

In your great majesty you tear down those who stand against you.
You send out your anger, and it burns them up like dry straw.

A blast from your nose piled up the water.
The waves stood still like a wall.
The deep sea turned solid in its middle.

The enemy said, ‘I will run them down and seize them!
I will divide up the loot until I have my fill.
I will unsheathe my sword and destroy them with my own hand.’

You blew a breath, and the sea closed over them.
Like lead they went down in the mighty waters.

Among all the gods, Yahweh, who can compare with you?
No one else is so holy and glorious,
so fearful to praise, so full of wonders.

You stretched out your right hand,
and the ground opened and took them in.

With your faithful love{e} you led the people you bought back.
With your strength you guided them to your holy home.

The nations heard and shook with fear.
Pain gripped the people of Philistia.

Then the chiefs of Edom were frightened.
The rulers{f} of Moab trembled.
Everyone who lives in Canaan lost courage.

You will carry them in and plant them on the mountain that is yours,
the spot, Yahweh, that you prepared as your home,
the holy place, Lord,{h} that your own hands made.
Yahweh is king for ever and ever.”
Pharaoh’s horses went into the sea with his chariots and his horsemen, and Yahweh turned the water back to cover them. Yet the Israelites crossed through the middle of the sea on dry ground.
Miriam,{i} a prophet and the sister of Aaron, took up a tambourine. Every woman came out after her, with tambourines and dancing.

Miriam sang the chorus back to them:
“Sing to Yahweh, for he has triumphed gloriously!
Rider and horse alike he flung into the waves.”
Moses then moved Israel on from the Red Sea. They entered the Desert of Shur{j} and walked for three days without finding any water.
They arrived at Marah, where the water was undrinkable because of its bitter taste. For this reason the place was named Marah.{k}
The people grumbled against Moses. “What are we supposed to drink?” they said.

Moses cried out to Yahweh, who pointed out a piece of wood.{l} Moses tossed it into the pool, and the bitter water became fresh and sweet. At that spot Yahweh{m} set down a rule and a law for the people. There too he tested them.

He said, “If you will truly listen to Yahweh your God, do what he sees as right, give heed to his commands, and obey all his rules, then none of the diseases I put on Egypt will fall on you. I am Yahweh, the one who heals you.”{n}
Next they reached Elim.{o} Twelve springs flowed there, and seventy palm trees grew around them. The people set up camp by the water.

notes.text: Hebrew “for he is highly lifted up.” The Hebrew repeats the verb to stress it.
Or “its chariot driver.”
Yah is a short form of Yahweh. It appears here for the first time. It is also heard in the word hallelujah, which means “praise Yah.”
Or “my power.” The first half of this verse is repeated in Isaiah 12:2 and Psalm 118:14.
Hebrew hesed, a faithful love that stays true to a promise.
Hebrew “rams,” a picture word for leaders or strong men.
Or “made.”
Hebrew Adonai. Many Hebrew copies and the Samaritan Pentateuch say “Yahweh.”
The meaning of Miriam is uncertain. Suggestions include “bitter,” “beloved,” and “rebellious.” In the New Testament the Greek form of her name is Mariam, or Mary.
Shur means “wall.” It may be named for a line of Egyptian border forts.
Marah means “bitter.”
Or “a tree.”
Hebrew “he.”
Hebrew Yahweh rofe’ekha. Later writers made a name out of it, “Yahweh Rophe,” which means “Yahweh who heals.”
Elim means “large trees.”

verses.text: Israel’s whole community set out from Elim and reached the Desert of Sin,{a} a region between Elim and Sinai. By then, a month and a half had passed since they left Egypt: it was the fifteenth day of the second month (April–May).{b}
Out in that wasteland, everyone in the community began grumbling at Moses and Aaron.

The Israelites said, “We wish Yahweh had struck us dead in Egypt! At least we sat by the meat pots there and ate bread until we were full. You have marched us into this wasteland so that the whole crowd will die of hunger.”

Then Yahweh spoke to Moses. “Watch,” he said. “Bread will fall from the sky like rain, for your benefit. Each day the people are to go out and gather just a day’s supply. By this I will find out whether they follow my instructions.
On the sixth day, what they bring home to prepare will be double what they collect on other days.”
Moses and Aaron told all Israel, “By this evening you will realize that Yahweh was the one who led you out of Egypt.
At dawn you will see the glory of Yahweh, because he has listened to your grumbling against him. Who are we, that you should grumble at us?”

Moses added, “Yahweh will provide meat for you to eat this evening, and at dawn he will fill you with bread. He has heard the grumbling you aimed at him. We are nobody. It is Yahweh you are grumbling at, not us.”
Moses said to Aaron, “Tell the entire community of Israel to step forward and stand before Yahweh, since he has heard what they are muttering.”
While Aaron was still talking to the whole community, they turned and looked into the desert. The glory of Yahweh was shining in the cloud.
Yahweh said to Moses,
“I have heard the Israelites grumbling. Give them this message: ‘By twilight{c} you will be eating meat, and by dawn you will be full of bread. Then you will realize that I, Yahweh, am your God.’”
That evening a huge flock of quail arrived and covered the camp. At daybreak dew lay on the ground around the tents.
When the dew evaporated, small flakes as fine as frost were left on the desert floor.
The Israelites noticed the flakes and asked each other, “What is it?”{d} They did not know what it was. Moses explained, “This is the bread that Yahweh is giving you for food.
Yahweh has given this order: Each person should collect what he or she can eat, about 2 quarts{e} per person. Bring home enough for everyone living in your tent.”
That is what the Israelites did, though some brought home more and some less.
Afterward they measured their portions.{f} The people with large amounts did not have extra, and the people with small amounts did not come up short. Each had collected just enough to eat.
“Nobody may save any of it for tomorrow morning,” Moses ordered.
A few people ignored Moses and saved some until the morning. It was crawling with worms and had a foul smell, and Moses became angry with them.
Every morning each person collected what he or she needed. Whatever stayed on the ground melted when the sun grew hot.
By the sixth day they were collecting twice as much, about 4 quarts{g} each. The community’s leaders came to Moses with the news.

He answered, “Here is what Yahweh has ordered: Tomorrow is a Sabbath,{h} a holy day of rest for Yahweh. Bake whatever you plan to bake today and boil whatever you plan to boil. Whatever is left over, store it away until morning.”
So they stored it overnight, as Moses had directed. It had no bad smell, and worms did not get into it.
Moses told them, “Today is a Sabbath for Yahweh, so eat what you have. You will not come across any of it out in the fields today.
Six days a week you may collect it. On the seventh day, the Sabbath, none will be there.”
Even so, a few of the people walked out on the seventh day looking for some. There was none to be found.
Yahweh said to Moses, “How long will all of you keep refusing to follow my commands and my teachings?

You see that Yahweh has made the Sabbath a gift to you. This explains why, on the sixth day, he supplies two days’ worth of bread. On the seventh day each one of you should stay put and not go anywhere.”
And the people did rest on that seventh day.
Israel’s people gave the bread the name manna.{i} It looked like small white coriander seeds, and it had a taste like honey wafers.

Moses said, “This is Yahweh’s command: Keep about 2 quarts{j} of manna for the generations to come, so that they can look at the food I supplied for you in the wilderness after I led you out of Egypt.”
Moses told Aaron, “Take a jar and put 2 quarts of manna in it. Place it in front of Yahweh to be kept for your descendants.”
Following Yahweh’s command to Moses, Aaron set the jar down in front of the Testimony,{k} where it would be preserved.
For forty years the Israelites lived on manna, up to the time they arrived in a settled country. They ate it right up to the edge of Canaan.
(The daily portion of about 2 quarts was a tenth of the standard dry measure of about three-fifths of a bushel.){l}

notes.text: Here Sin is a place name. It has nothing to do with the English word “sin.” It may be related to the name Sinai.

Hebrew “the fifteenth day of the second month,” counted from the spring new year (see the note at 12:2). The second month was later called Iyyar, or Ziv in 1 Kings 6:1. It fell in April–May, a month after leaving Egypt (12:18).
Hebrew “between the two evenings.” See the note at 12:6.
Hebrew man hu, “What is it?” The question explains the name manna (verse 31).
Hebrew “an omer.” An omer was about 2 dry quarts (2.2 liters). See verse 36.
Hebrew “when they measured it with the omer.”
Hebrew “two omers,” about 4 dry quarts (4.4 liters).
Hebrew shabbaton shabbat-qodesh, “a rest, a holy Sabbath.” Sabbath comes from shavat, “to stop” or “to rest.” This is the first time the word appears in the Bible.
Hebrew man, “What?” (see verse 15). Numbers 11:7–9 also describes it.
Hebrew “an omerful.” The same word is used in verse 33.
That is, in front of the ark that would hold the tablets of the Testimony (25:16, 21–22). The writer speaks of a practice that came later.
Hebrew “the omer is a tenth of the ephah.” An omer was about 2.2 liters (2 dry quarts) and an ephah about 22 liters (three-fifths of a bushel). Ancient standards varied.

verses.text: The whole community of Israel left the Desert of Sin and moved from place to place as Yahweh directed.{a} They camped at Rephidim,{b} but there was no drinking water there.
The people quarreled with Moses and said, “Give us water to drink!” Moses answered, “What makes you quarrel with me? Are you trying to put Yahweh on trial?”
Thirst made the people bitter against Moses. “What was the point of bringing us up from Egypt?” they grumbled. “Do you mean to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”
Moses cried out to Yahweh, “What can I do with these people? They are almost ready to stone me!”
Yahweh told Moses, “Go forward, ahead of the people, and bring some of the elders of Israel along. Carry the stick you used when you struck the Nile.
I will be waiting for you there on a rock at Horeb. Hit that rock, and water will flow out so the people can drink.” Moses followed these orders with the elders of Israel looking on.
He called the place Massah and Meribah,{c} since the Israelites had quarreled there and tested Yahweh by asking, “Is Yahweh in our midst, or not?”
At Rephidim, the Amalekites{d} marched out and fought against Israel.
Moses told Joshua,{e} “Pick out some men, and go to war against Amalek. I will take my place on the hilltop tomorrow with the stick of God in my hand.”
Joshua did what Moses ordered and fought Amalek. Moses, Aaron, and Hur{f} went up to the top of the hill.
As long as Moses kept his hand in the air, Israel gained ground. When he let it fall, Amalek gained ground.
But Moses’ arms got heavy. Aaron and Hur rolled a stone over for him to sit on, and then stood on either side of him, each supporting one hand. So his hands did not shake before sunset.
In this way Joshua defeated the Amalekite army with the sword.{g}
Yahweh said to Moses, “Write this down in a book{h} so it will be remembered, and tell it to Joshua. I will wipe out every memory of Amalek from under the sky.”
Moses built an altar and called it Yahweh Nissi,{i}
because he said, “Lift your hand toward the throne of Yah!{j} Yahweh will fight Amalek in every generation.”

notes.text: Hebrew “by the mouth of Yahweh.”
Rephidim may mean “resting places.” No one knows where it was.
Massah means “testing,” and Meribah means “arguing.”
Amalek was a desert nation that came from Esau’s grandson Amalek (Genesis 36:12).
Joshua appears here for the first time. His Hebrew name, Yehoshua, means “Yahweh saves.” He was first called Hoshea, “salvation” (Numbers 13:16). The Greek form of Joshua is Iesous, or Jesus.
Hur may mean “child,” or it may come from the Egyptian god Horus. Jewish tradition says he was Miriam’s husband. See also 24:14.
Hebrew “by the mouth of the sword.”
Or “on a scroll.” Hebrew sefer means any written record.
Yahweh Nissi means “Yahweh is my banner.” A banner was a pole raised as a rallying point in battle, like Moses’ raised stick.

The Hebrew is hard to read. It may mean “a hand raised toward the throne of Yah,” or it may be an oath. If the word kes (“throne”) is read as nes (“banner”), it means “a hand on the banner of Yah,” which fits the name Yahweh Nissi. The Septuagint says “with a hidden hand the Lord fights against Amalek.” See the note at 15:2 on Yah.

subheads.14: An altar named for a banner

verses.text: Moses’ father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian, was told about all that God had done for Moses and for Israel his people, and how Yahweh had led Israel out of Egypt.
Zipporah had gone back to her father at an earlier time, sent away by Moses.{a} Now Jethro took her along,
and with her two sons. The first was called Gershom, since Moses had said, “I am a stranger living in a land that is not mine.”
The second was called Eliezer,{b} since Moses had also said, “My father’s God came to my aid and rescued me when Pharaoh wanted to kill me.”
Jethro, with Moses’ wife and sons, came to Moses in the desert, at the mountain of God where he had camped.
He had a message sent to Moses:{c} “It is your father-in-law Jethro. I am on my way to you, with your wife and her two sons beside me.”

So Moses walked out to greet his father-in-law. Bending low, he kissed the older man, and the two asked how each other was doing. After that they went into Moses’ tent, where Moses began to tell the whole story.
Moses told his father-in-law all that Yahweh had done to Pharaoh and Egypt for Israel’s sake. He told about every hardship they had met on the way and how Yahweh had rescued them.
Jethro was thrilled about all the kind things Yahweh had done for Israel, especially the rescue from the Egyptians.
He said, “Praise Yahweh! He has saved you from the Egyptians and from Pharaoh. He has set these people free from Egyptian power.
Now I know that Yahweh is greater than all other gods, for he proved it when the Egyptians treated Israel with such pride.”{d}
Then Jethro brought a burnt offering and other sacrifices for God. Aaron arrived with all of Israel’s elders, and they shared a meal with Moses’ father-in-law in the presence of God.
The next day Moses took his seat to settle disputes among the people. They stood around him from morning until evening.
When Jethro saw how much Moses was doing for the people, he asked, “Why are you handling all this? Why are you sitting here alone while the people stand around you from sunrise to sunset?”
Moses told him, “They come to me when they want God’s guidance.
When two people have an argument, they bring it to me. I decide who is right, and I teach them God’s rules and instructions.”
Moses’ father-in-law replied, “This is not the right way to do it.
You will exhaust yourself, and so will all these people. The task is heavier than you can carry, and you cannot manage it by yourself.
Now take my advice, and may God be with you. You stand before God on behalf of the people, and you bring their problems to him.
Teach the people God’s rules and instructions. Show them the path they should follow and the duties they should carry out.

Beyond that, pick out capable men from among everyone: men who honor God, who are honest, and who will not accept money to bend the truth. Appoint them as officials over groups of a thousand, a hundred, fifty, and ten.

These men should serve as the people’s judges all the time. They will bring you every serious case, but the small ones they can settle on their own. Then your burden will be lighter, since they will carry part of it with you.
If you follow this plan and God approves, you will be able to keep going, and everyone here will return to their homes at peace.”
Moses listened to his father-in-law and did everything he suggested.
Moses selected capable men out of the whole nation and put them in charge of the people, as officials over a thousand, a hundred, fifty, and ten.{e}
They served as judges for the people at every hour. Hard cases went to Moses, while they took care of the small ones on their own.
Moses then sent his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro returned to his own land.

notes.text: Hebrew shilluheha, “her sending away.” The text does not say when or why Moses sent her back. The last time she is mentioned is 4:20–26.
Eliezer means “my God is help.”
This follows the Hebrew. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, and the Syriac say, “Someone told Moses, ‘Look, your father-in-law Jethro is coming to you.’”
The Hebrew at the end of this verse is short and hard to understand. A word-for-word version is “for in the thing in which they acted proudly against them.”
The Samaritan Pentateuch adds a passage here taken from Deuteronomy 1:9–18, where Moses tells in his own words how the judges were chosen.

verses.text: In the third month (May–June){a} after Israel left Egypt, on the first day of that month,{b} the people came into the Desert of Sinai.
Having set out from Rephidim, they entered the Sinai desert and pitched their tents there, right at the mountain’s base.
Moses went up the mountain to God, and Yahweh called out to him there. “Tell the house of Jacob, the descendants of Israel, what I say:
You have seen with your own eyes how I dealt with Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.
If you will listen closely to me and hold to my agreement, then out of all nations you will be mine, my own treasure.{c} The whole earth is mine,
yet you will be priests who serve me, a people set apart. Pass these words along to the Israelites.”
Moses returned and called the leaders of the people together. He told them everything Yahweh had ordered him to say.
All the people answered at once: “We will do everything Yahweh has said.” Moses took their answer back to Yahweh.

Yahweh said to Moses, “Listen, I will come to you inside a dense cloud. The people will hear when I talk with you, and they will trust you from then on.” Moses carried the people’s reply back to Yahweh.
Yahweh said to Moses, “Go to the people and prepare them today and tomorrow. They are to wash their clothes
