and stand ready for day three. On that day Yahweh will descend onto Mount Sinai in plain view of all the people.
Set limits around the mountain for the people and say, ‘Take care! Do not go up the mountain, and do not touch the foot of it. Whoever lays a finger on it will certainly die.

No one is to lay a hand on such a person. Stones or arrows must kill him, whether he is a man or an animal. He cannot be allowed to live.’ Only when the ram’s horn{d} gives one long blast may the people go up the mountain.”
So Moses left the mountain and went to the people and made them ready. They washed their clothes.
“Be ready on the third day,” he told them. “Until then, stay away from your wives.”
At dawn on the third day there was thunder and lightning, and a heavy cloud rested on the mountain. A blast from a trumpet rang out, very loud, and everyone in the camp trembled.
Next Moses brought the people out of camp to meet God. They took their places at the base of the mountain.
Smoke covered all of Mount Sinai, because Yahweh had landed on it in fire. The smoke climbed like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain{e} shook hard.
The trumpet grew louder and louder. Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice like thunder.{f}
Yahweh descended to the peak of Mount Sinai and summoned Moses to the peak. So Moses went up.
Yahweh told him, “Go down and warn the people. They must not break through toward Yahweh to gaze at him, or a great many will die.
The priests, too, who approach Yahweh, need to purify themselves, or Yahweh will break out against them.”
Moses said to Yahweh, “The people cannot climb Mount Sinai. You yourself warned us. You told us to mark a boundary around the mountain and keep it holy.”
“Go down,” Yahweh told him, “and then return with Aaron. But the priests and the people must not force their way up to Yahweh. He would strike them down.”
So Moses went down to the people and told them.

notes.text: Hebrew “in the third month,” later called Sivan, counted from the spring new year (see the note at 12:2). It fell in May–June.
Literally “on this day.” It probably means the first day of the month, at the new moon.
Hebrew segullah, a person’s own treasure, like a king’s private property.
Hebrew yovel, “ram’s horn.” The trumpet (shofar) in verses 16 and 19 is a different word for a similar instrument.
The Septuagint and some Hebrew copies say “the whole people.”
Or “in thunder.” The Hebrew word qol means both “voice” and “thunder.”

subheads.1: At the foot of Mount Sinai
subheads.16: Thunder and fire on the mountain

verses.text: Then God spoke all these words:{a}
“I am Yahweh, your God, who led you out of slavery in Egypt.
Do not worship any god except me.{b}
Make no idol{c} for yourselves, no statue shaped like anything in the sky, on the ground, or in the waters below.

You must neither kneel to such things nor serve them. I, Yahweh your God, demand your whole love.{d} If parents reject me, their children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren suffer for it, as long as they also reject me.
But toward those who love me and keep my commands, I show faithful love{e} for a thousand generations.
Never use the name of Yahweh your God in a way that is false or empty.{f} Yahweh will hold guilty anyone who misuses his name.
Keep the Sabbath day in mind, and treat it as holy.
For six days you work and finish all your jobs.

But the seventh day is a Sabbath for Yahweh your God. On it, none of you may do any work: not you, not your son or daughter, not your male or female servants, not your animals, and not the foreigner living in your towns.
In six days Yahweh made the sky, the land, the sea, and all that fills them, and on the seventh day he rested. This is why he blessed the Sabbath and made it holy.
Show respect to both your father and your mother. Then you will live long in the land Yahweh your God gives you.
Never commit murder.{g}
Never betray your husband or wife.
Do not steal.
Never give false testimony against another person.
Never crave the house{h} that belongs to someone near you. Never crave that person’s wife, servants, ox, donkey, or anything else he owns.”
Thunder boomed and lightning flashed. A trumpet sounded and the mountain smoked, and when the people saw all this, they backed away trembling and stood at a distance.
“You talk to us, and we will listen,” they told Moses. “God must not speak to us, or we will die.”
Moses told the people, “Stop being afraid. God has come to put you to the test, so that fear of him will stay with you and keep you from sin.”
The people stayed far away, while Moses went up to the thick darkness where God was.{i}
Yahweh said to Moses, “Tell the Israelites this: You have seen it yourselves. I have spoken to you from the sky.
Do not make gods of silver or gold to be placed beside me.
Build an altar of earth for me, and place your burnt offerings and fellowship offerings{j} on it, whether sheep, goats, or cattle. Wherever I have my name honored, I will come and bless you.
If you build me a stone altar, use rough stones as they are. A stone you have worked with a tool becomes unfit.
Do not use steps to climb up to my altar, so that no one’s nakedness is exposed.

notes.text: The Ten Commandments are called “the ten words” in Hebrew (34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13). They are given again in Deuteronomy 5:6–21 with a few differences. Jewish and Christian traditions number them in different ways.
Or “besides me,” or “in defiance of me.” Hebrew “before my face.”
Hebrew pesel, an idol carved from wood or stone or cast in metal.
Hebrew El qanna, “a jealous God,” one who wants a faithful relationship, as a husband does in marriage. See 34:14, where Qanna is used as a name.
Or “to the thousandth generation,” which is far greater than the third and fourth generation of verse 5. Compare Deuteronomy 7:9. On “faithful love,” see the note at 15:13.
Or “Do not misuse the name.” The command forbids using God’s name to support a lie, such as a false oath, or for worthless purposes.

Hebrew ratsah, killing that is against the law. The word is not used for killing in war or for a lawful execution. The Septuagint (Vaticanus) gives verses 13–15 in the order “Do not commit adultery. Do not steal. Do not murder.”
After this verse the Samaritan Pentateuch adds a commandment, based on Deuteronomy 11:29–30 and 27:2–7, to build an altar on Mount Gerizim.
In verses 19–21 the Samaritan Pentateuch adds passages taken from Deuteronomy 5:24–31 and 18:18–22, including the promise of a prophet like Moses.
Hebrew shelamim, offerings for fellowship, thanksgiving, or vows, shared among the worshiper, the priests, and God.

subheads.14: Do not be unfaithful in marriage

verses.text: Here are the legal rulings{a} that you must put before the people:
If you purchase a Hebrew slave,{b} his service lasts six years. During the seventh he walks out a free man and pays nothing.
If he arrived single, he goes out single. If he arrived with a wife, she goes out with him.
Now suppose his master provided him a wife, and she had sons or daughters. Then she and her children remain the master’s, and the man goes out alone.
But the slave may declare, “My master, my wife, and my children are dear to me. I refuse to go free.”
If so, his master brings him before God.{c} There, at the door or doorframe, the master drives an awl through the slave’s ear, and the man serves him for the rest of his life.
If a man sells his daughter into service, she does not go free in the way male servants do.
If her master picked her for himself and then is displeased with her, he must let her family buy her back. He has no right to sell her to foreigners, since he broke faith with her.
If he gave her to his son, he must treat her as he would a daughter.
Should he take another wife as well, he may not reduce the first woman’s food, clothing, or marital rights.
If he fails her in any of these three, she may go free, and no payment is required.
Death is the penalty for anyone who strikes a person dead.
If the killing was not planned, however, and God allowed it to happen, then I will name a place for the killer to flee to.
When someone deliberately plots to kill his neighbor, he is to be dragged away, even from my altar, and executed.
Death is also the penalty for striking one’s father or mother.
A person who kidnaps someone, whether he sells him or is found still holding him, must be put to death.
Likewise, anyone who curses a father or mother is to be executed.
Say two men are quarreling. One of them hits the other, using a rock or his fist. The victim lives but is kept in bed.
Once he is on his feet and can get around outside with his staff, the attacker is not punished. He does owe the victim for his lost work time, and he must see that he is fully healed.
A slave, male or female, may be beaten with a rod by the owner. If the slave dies right then, the owner must be punished.{d}
Yet if the slave lingers a day or two before dying, the owner goes unpunished, because the slave was his own property.

Suppose men are fighting and they strike a pregnant woman so that she gives birth early, yet she is not otherwise hurt. The one at fault pays whatever fine the woman’s husband demands, as the judges approve.
But if she is harmed, the penalty is life for life,
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
scorching for scorching, gash for gash, welt for welt.
If an owner hits the eye of his slave, whether a man or a woman, and ruins it, he sets that slave free as compensation for the eye.
And if the owner knocks out a slave’s tooth, male or female, the slave goes free as compensation for the tooth.
If an ox kills a man or a woman by goring, the ox must be stoned, and no one may eat its meat. Its owner is not to be blamed.
But if the ox had a habit of goring, its owner was warned, and he still did not pen it up, then when it kills a man or woman, the ox is stoned and its owner is also put to death.
If a ransom is set for the owner instead, he must pay whatever sum is demanded to save his life.
This same ruling applies if the ox gores a son or daughter.
If the ox kills a slave, male or female, the owner of the ox pays the slave’s master thirty shekels of silver (about 12 ounces, or 345 grams),{e} and the ox is stoned.
Suppose a man removes the lid from a pit, or digs one and leaves it uncovered, and someone’s ox or donkey tumbles into it.
the pit’s owner must pay for the loss. He gives the animal’s owner its value in money and keeps the dead animal.
When one man’s ox injures another man’s ox and kills it, the owners sell the living ox and share the money. They also share the carcass.
But if it was known that the ox gored in the past and its owner kept it penned up poorly, he must replace the ox with an ox, and the dead animal becomes his.

notes.text: Hebrew mishpatim, “case laws” or “judgments.” These laws (21:1–23:19) are often called the Book of the Covenant (24:7). They are written as cases: “If someone does this, then this is done.”
Or “Hebrew servant.” Hebrew eved means “slave” or “servant,” depending on the setting. This law covers a debt-servant. Compare Leviticus 25:39–46 and Deuteronomy 15:12–18.
Or “to the judges.” Hebrew elohim can mean God, gods, or judges. It probably means taking the man to the local sanctuary to swear an oath.
Hebrew “he shall be avenged.” The word is not defined, but it probably refers to the death penalty in verse 12.
Hebrew “thirty shekels of silver.” A shekel weighed about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), so thirty shekels was about 12 ounces (345 grams).

verses.text: The penalty for stealing an ox or a sheep{a} and then killing or selling it is heavy: five oxen to replace the ox, four sheep to replace the sheep.
A burglar is caught breaking in and is struck dead. No guilt for bloodshed falls on the one who struck him.
But if it happened after sunrise, the defender is guilty of murder. A thief is required to pay in full. If he has nothing, he must be sold to cover the theft.
Should the stolen animal turn up alive in his hands, be it an ox, donkey, or sheep, he repays twice its value.
A man may turn his animals loose to graze, and they eat from someone else’s field or vineyard. He compensates the owner with the finest crops from his own land.{b}
Say a fire breaks out and catches in thorn hedges, burning stacked grain, uncut grain, or a whole field. The one who lit the fire must pay for every loss.
If a person leaves silver or valuables with a neighbor for safekeeping and they are stolen from the neighbor’s house, the thief, if caught, must repay double.
If no thief turns up, the house owner must go before God{c} so that it can be decided whether he took his neighbor’s goods himself.

In any dispute about ownership, whether the item is an ox, donkey, sheep, clothing, or some lost thing, and one person says, “That is mine,” both must bring their case before God. The party whom God finds guilty{d} repays the other twice over.
Imagine a man hands his neighbor a donkey, ox, sheep, or another animal for safekeeping, and it dies, is hurt, or is driven off with no witness.
Then Yahweh’s oath is to settle it between them: the neighbor swears he has not laid a hand on the other man’s property. The owner must accept this, and no payment is made.
If, though, the animal was actually stolen from the neighbor’s care, he pays the owner back.
If a wild animal ripped it to pieces, he brings the remains as evidence. He owes nothing for the mauled animal.
Suppose a man borrows his neighbor’s animal, and it is hurt or dies while its owner is absent. The borrower pays in full.
If the owner was there with it, no payment is due. If the animal was hired, the hire price covers the loss.{e}
When a man persuades a young woman who is not engaged to sleep with him, he must pay the bride price{f} and make her his wife.
Should her father absolutely refuse to let him marry her, the man still pays the standard bride price for a young woman.
A woman who practices sorcery must not be allowed to live.
Whoever has sex with an animal must be executed.
The person who offers sacrifices to any god other than Yahweh must be destroyed.{g}
Foreigners among you are not to be wronged or oppressed. Remember that you yourselves lived as foreigners in Egypt.
Never mistreat a widow or an orphan.
If you wrong such people and they appeal to me, I will surely hear their cry.
My anger will blaze up, and I will kill you with the sword. Your wives will be left widows, and your children will lose their father.
When you lend money to a poor person among my people, do not behave like a lender who profits from him. Charge him no interest.
If you accept a neighbor’s coat as a pledge, return it to him by sundown,
since it is the only blanket he has. What else can he sleep in? If he calls to me for help, I will hear him, because I am compassionate.
You must not insult God,{h} and you must not curse any ruler over your people.
Do not be slow to give me the first part of your harvest and of your pressed wine and oil.{i} Give me your firstborn sons.
Treat your cattle and sheep the same way. A newborn stays with its mother seven days, and on the eighth you give it to me.
You are to belong to me as holy people. So do not eat meat from an animal killed in the field by wild beasts. Throw it to the dogs.

notes.text: In the Hebrew text, verse 1 is numbered 21:37, and verses 2–31 are numbered 22:1–30.
The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint have a longer text: “He must pay for the damage from the best of his own field, or the best of the produce of his vineyard.”
Or “before the judges.” See the note at 21:6.
Or “whom the judges declare guilty.” The Hebrew verb is plural.
Or “if it was hired, he bears the loss of the hire price.” The Hebrew is very short, literally “if hired, it came for its hire.”
Hebrew mohar, a payment made by the groom to the bride’s family at marriage.
Hebrew herem, “set apart” for God, usually meaning set apart for destruction.
Or “the judges.” Hebrew elohim. Paul quotes the second half of this verse in Acts 23:5.
Hebrew “your fullness and your trickling,” meaning the first of the grain and the first of the wine and oil.

verses.text: Do not pass along false rumors. Do not team up with the wicked by lying as a witness for them.
Do not go along with the crowd when it does wrong. In a lawsuit, do not give testimony that follows the majority and twists justice.
Do not favor a poor person either, just because he is poor.
If your enemy’s ox or donkey strays and you find it, take it back to its owner.
When you see the donkey of someone who hates you collapsed under its load, do not walk past. You must stop and help him free it.{a}
Do not deny justice to the poor among you when they have a dispute.
Keep away from false charges. Do not cause the death of anyone innocent or in the right, because I will never declare a guilty person innocent.
Take no bribes. A bribe blinds people who can see and twists the words of honest people.
Never oppress a foreigner. You understand{b} what it is like, having been foreigners yourselves in Egypt.
For six years sow your fields and bring in their crops.

But in the seventh year, give the land a rest and let it lie fallow. The poor of your people can eat what grows, and the wild animals can have the leftovers. Treat your vineyard and olive grove the same way.
Six days are for your work. The seventh is for rest, so your ox and donkey can relax, and your servant and the foreigner can be refreshed.
Take care to follow all I have told you. Never invoke the names of other gods. They are not to be heard coming from your mouth.
Three times every year you are to hold a festival for me.

Observe the Festival of Unleavened Bread. As I ordered you, eat bread made without yeast for a week. Do it in the month of Abib (March–April),{c} the month when you left Egypt. Nobody should appear before me with empty hands.

Keep the Harvest Festival,{d} to celebrate the first of the crops you have planted in your fields. Keep the Festival of Gathering{e} at the end of the year, when you bring in the harvest from your fields.
Three times a year every man among you is to appear before the Lord Yahweh.{f}
Do not offer the blood of a sacrifice to me together with anything made with yeast. Do not leave the fat from my festival offering until morning.
Bring the best of the first crops from your land to the house of Yahweh your God. Do not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.{g}
I am about to send an angel in front of you. He will guard you on your journey and take you to the place I have made ready.
Respect him and listen to him. Do not defy him, for he will not pardon your rebellion. My name is within him.
But if you listen carefully to his voice and do all I say, I will fight against your enemies and oppose those who oppose you.
My angel goes ahead of you. He will bring you to the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hivites, and Jebusites, and I will destroy them all.
Do not bow to their gods, worship them, or copy their practices. Instead, you must tear their idols down and smash their sacred stones to pieces.
Worship Yahweh your God, and he will bless your bread and water. I will remove illness from your midst.
In your land no woman will lose a baby or be unable to have children. I will give you a full lifetime.
I will send terror ahead of you and throw every nation you meet into panic. I will make all your enemies turn and run.
I will send the hornets{h} ahead to push the Hivites, Canaanites, and Hittites out from your path.
It will not happen in one year. If it did, the land would be left deserted, and wild animals would grow too many for you.
Little by little I will force them out as you increase, until you are numerous enough to possess the land.

Your territory will stretch from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean,{i} and from the southern desert to the Euphrates River.{j} I will put the land’s inhabitants in your power, and you will drive them off before you.
You are not to make a treaty with them or their gods.
Do not let them stay in your country. They would make you sin against me, and serving their gods would be a deadly snare for you.

notes.text: The Hebrew is hard to understand. Literally it reads, “you shall cease from leaving it to him; you shall surely release with him.”
Hebrew nefesh, “soul,” “life,” or “inner feelings.”
Hebrew “the month of Abib.” See the note at 13:4.
That is, the wheat harvest in late spring, later called the Festival of Weeks.
That is, the autumn harvest of fruit and olives, later called the Festival of Booths.
Hebrew ha’adon YHWH, “the Lord, Yahweh.” Here Adon (“Lord” or “Master”) is a title and Yahweh is the name.
This command is repeated in 34:26 and Deuteronomy 14:21. It may have forbidden a pagan ritual practice.
Or “panic” or “plague.” The meaning of the Hebrew word tsir’ah is uncertain. See Deuteronomy 7:20; Joshua 24:12.
Hebrew “the Sea of the Philistines,” the Mediterranean Sea.
Hebrew “the River,” the Euphrates.

verses.text: God told Moses, “Climb up to Yahweh, you and Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy of Israel’s leaders. Bow down in worship from a distance.
Moses alone is to approach Yahweh. The others must stay back, and the people are not to climb with him.”
Moses came and reported to the people everything Yahweh had said, including the rulings. They all answered together, “We will do every single thing Yahweh has told us.”
Moses then wrote down all of Yahweh’s words. Early next morning he built an altar at the base of the mountain and set up twelve stone pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.
He sent some young Israelite men to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice bulls as fellowship offerings to Yahweh.
Moses poured half the blood into bowls and splashed the other half against the altar.
Next he picked up the Book of the Covenant and read it out for the people to hear. They answered, “We will do all that Yahweh has said, and we will listen to him.”
Moses scooped up the blood and threw it on the people, saying, “Here is the blood that seals the agreement{a} Yahweh has made with you, based on all these words.”
Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy of Israel’s leaders then went up.
There they saw the God of Israel.{b} Under his feet was something like a floor of deep blue stone,{c} bright as the sky itself.
Yet God did not raise his hand against these Israelite leaders.{d} They gazed at God, then ate a meal and drank together.
Then Yahweh spoke to Moses: “Ascend the mountain and join me, and stay. I will hand you stone tablets inscribed with the teaching and commands I have written for the people’s instruction.”
So Moses set out with Joshua, his assistant, and climbed God’s mountain.
To the leaders he said, “Stay put until we return to you. Aaron and Hur are here with you, and anyone with a dispute can go to them.”
Moses climbed, and the cloud covered the mountain.
Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and for six days the cloud hid the mountain. Then, on day seven, Yahweh summoned Moses out of the cloud.
To the Israelites, the glory of Yahweh looked like a blazing fire on the mountaintop.
Moses walked into the cloud and went up the mountain. He stayed there forty days and forty nights.

notes.text: Hebrew “the blood of the covenant.” A covenant is a binding agreement. Jesus echoes these words at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:28; Mark 14:24). Compare Hebrews 9:18–20.
The Septuagint reads “they saw the place where the God of Israel stood,” and in verse 11 “they appeared in the place of God,” which softens the statement that they saw God.
Or “sapphire.” The ancient sapphire was probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone.
Hebrew atsilim, “corners” or “nobles,” a rare word.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“Tell the Israelites to bring me a contribution.{a} Collect it from every person whose heart moves him to give.
These are the gifts you may accept from them: gold, silver, and bronze;{b}
yarn dyed blue, purple, and scarlet,{c} plus fine linen and goat’s hair;
ram skins stained red, fine leather,{d} and acacia wood;{e}
lamp oil; spices to blend into the anointing oil and the fragrant incense;
and onyx stones{f} and other gems to mount on the ephod{g} and the breastpiece.
Have them build me a holy place, so that I can live among them.
Make the dwelling{h} and all its furnishings exactly like the pattern I am about to show you.
Build a chest{i} from acacia wood. Its length is to be 45 inches, and its width and height 27 inches each.{j}
Gold goes over every surface, inside and out, and a gold border runs around the top edge.
Cast four rings of gold and attach them to the four feet, placing two rings on each long side.
Carrying poles come next, made of acacia wood and gold-plated.
Slide those poles into the rings along the chest’s sides, so the chest can be lifted and carried.
Leave the poles in their rings. They must never be taken out.
In the chest you will put the stone tablets{k} I am going to give you.
For the top, make a cover of pure gold, 45 inches by 27 inches.{l}
Hammer out two winged creatures{m} of gold and set them at the two ends of the cover.
Make them as one piece with the cover, one at each end.
Their wings are to be spread upward, shading the cover, and they are to face each other, looking down toward it.
Place the cover over the chest, and lay inside the chest the tablets that are to be given to you.
At that cover, between the two winged creatures that stand over the chest of the tablets, I will meet you. From that spot I will tell you everything I want the Israelites to do.
Now construct a table out of acacia wood. It should stand 27 inches high, with a top 36 inches long and 18 inches wide.{n}
Plate it with pure gold and run a gold border around its edge.
Fit a rim about 3 inches wide{o} all around it, with a gold border on the rim.
Cast four gold rings and fix them to the four corners, at the top of the four legs.
The rings sit right beside the rim and hold the poles that are used to lift the table.
Cut the poles from acacia and coat them in gold. People will carry the table with them.
Also fashion its plates, dishes, jars, and bowls for the pouring of drink offerings, using pure gold.
On the table, keep the bread of the Presence{p} in front of me, always.
Make a lampstand{q} of pure gold, hammered out, with its base and shaft. Its cups, buds, and flowers{r} are all to be made as one piece with it.
Six branches are to reach out from the stem, three branching from the left side and three from the right.
Each branch is to have three cups shaped like almond blossoms, with a bud and a flower on every cup. This is true for all six branches.
On the lampstand’s shaft there are to be four cups shaped like almond blossoms, each with its bud and flower.
A bud is to be under each pair of the six branches that extend from the lampstand.
The buds and branches must be a single piece with the lampstand, all of it beaten from one lump of pure gold.
Make seven lamps for it, and mount them so that they shine on the area in front of the stand.
Its wick trimmers and trays are also to be pure gold.
Use about 75 pounds of pure gold{s} for the lampstand and all its tools.
Take care that you build each item to match the pattern shown to you on the mountain.”

notes.text: Hebrew terumah, a contribution set apart, literally “something lifted off.”
Or “copper.” Hebrew nehoshet means copper or its alloy, bronze.
The colors came from dyes: blue (or violet) from sea snails, purple from murex shells, and scarlet from an insect dye.
Hebrew tahash. The meaning is uncertain. Suggestions include the skins of dolphins or dugongs (sea cows), goatskin, or leather dyed a particular color.
Acacia is a hard, durable desert wood that grows in Sinai.
Or “carnelian.” The identification of many ancient stones is uncertain.
The ephod was an outer priestly garment, apparently a kind of apron or vest (28:6–14).
Hebrew mishkan, “dwelling place,” from shakan, “to dwell” (verse 8). It was a portable tent-shrine, often called the tabernacle.
Hebrew aron, “chest” or “box,” a different word from Noah’s ark. It is often called the ark of the covenant.

Hebrew “two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high.” A cubit, the distance from elbow to fingertip, was about 18 inches (45 centimeters), so the chest was about 45 by 27 by 27 inches. A longer cubit of about 20.5 inches (52 centimeters) was also used, and the sizes in these chapters may be somewhat larger.
Hebrew ha’edut, “the testimony,” the two stone tablets that bore witness to the covenant (31:18).
Hebrew kapporet, from the verb kipper, “to atone” or “to cover.” It is traditionally called the “mercy seat.” The measurement is “two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide.”
Hebrew keruvim, cherubim (singular cherub), winged heavenly beings often pictured in the ancient Near East as guardians of thrones and holy places. Compare Genesis 3:24.
Hebrew “two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high.”
Hebrew “a handbreadth,” about 3 inches (7.5 centimeters).
Literally “bread of the face,” twelve loaves set before Yahweh and renewed every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9).
Hebrew menorah.
Hebrew kaftor, probably the bulb or base of the flower.
Hebrew “a talent of pure gold.” A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).

verses.text: “The dwelling itself is to be made from ten curtains of finely spun linen, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn. Have skilled workers embroider winged creatures{a} on them.
Each curtain is to measure 42 feet by 6 feet,{b} all the same size.
Join five of the curtains into one set, and five into another.
Sew loops of blue fabric onto the selvage of the final curtain in every set.
Make fifty loops on the first curtain and fifty on the edge of the last curtain of the other set, so that the loops line up.
Make fifty gold clasps and use them to join the two sets, so that the dwelling becomes one whole.
Next, make a covering for the dwelling from eleven curtains of goat hair.
Each of these is to be 45 feet by 6 feet,{c} all the same size.
Join five of these curtains into one piece and the other six into a second piece. The sixth curtain is to be doubled over in front of the tent.
Put fifty loops along the edge of the end curtain of one piece, and fifty along the edge of the end curtain of the second piece.
Make fifty bronze clasps. Fit them into the loops to join the covering into a single unit.
The extra half curtain is to hang down over the back of the dwelling.
The curtains will be a foot and a half too long on each side. That extra length is to hang down on both sides and cover the dwelling.{d}
Make two more coverings, one of ram skins dyed red and one of fine leather, to go over the top.
The upright frames{e} for the dwelling are to be made of acacia wood.
Every frame must stand 15 feet high and measure 27 inches across.{f}
Each frame gets two projections{g} that fit it to the one beside it. Make every frame in this manner.
Place twenty frames along the south side of the dwelling.
Under those twenty frames set forty silver bases,{h} two bases under each frame, one for each projection.
Build twenty frames for the north side too,
and forty more silver bases to go under them, a pair beneath each frame.
For the back, the west side, make six frames.
Make two more frames for the two back corners.
These are to be joined together at the bottom and fastened at the top to a single ring. Make both corner frames this way.{i}
So there will be eight frames in all, with sixteen silver bases, two under each frame.
Cut crossbars from acacia wood: five to hold together the frames on the first side of the dwelling,
five for the frames facing them across the tent, and five for the frames at the back, on the west.
The middle crossbar runs the full length, through the center of the frames.
Plate the frames in gold. Forge gold rings to hold the crossbars, and plate the bars as well.
Raise the dwelling to match the plan that was shown to you on the mountain.
Make an inner curtain{j} from blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen, with winged creatures stitched into it by a skilled worker.
It hangs on gold hooks fixed to four acacia posts that are plated with gold and stand on four silver bases.
Suspend this curtain from the clasps. Behind it put the chest of the tablets. This curtain divides the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.{k}
Set the cover on the chest of the tablets in the Most Holy Place.
Position the table in front of the curtain, on the dwelling’s north side. The lampstand goes across from it, on the south side.
For the entrance of the tent, weave a screen of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen, embroidered by a weaver.
For this screen make five acacia posts, plated with gold, with gold hooks. Cast five bronze bases to hold the posts.”

notes.text: Hebrew keruvim, winged heavenly beings. See the note at 25:18.
Hebrew “twenty-eight cubits” long and “four cubits” wide. On the cubit (18 inches), see the note at 25:10.
Hebrew “thirty cubits” long and “four cubits” wide.
Hebrew “a cubit,” about 18 inches (45 centimeters), on each side.
Hebrew qerashim, traditionally “boards.” They may have been open frameworks rather than solid planks.
Hebrew “ten cubits” tall and “a cubit and a half” wide. The sizes are about 4.5 meters by 0.7 meter.
Hebrew “hands,” projections that fit into the bases.
Or “sockets,” hollow bases into which the projections fit.
The construction of the corner frames is uncertain. The Hebrew can also mean “they will be double at the bottom and joined at the top.”
Hebrew parokhet, the inner curtain that closed off the Most Holy Place.
Hebrew “the holy of holies.”

subheads.1: The inner coverings of the tent

verses.text: “Build an altar of acacia wood, a square 7½ feet on each side and 4½ feet high.{a}
At each of its four corners make a horn{b} that is one piece with the altar, and cover the whole altar with bronze.
Make bronze pots for clearing away the ashes, and bronze shovels, basins, forks, and fire pans. All its tools are to be bronze.
Make a bronze grate for it, shaped like a net, with a bronze ring at each of its four corners.
Fit the grate halfway down inside the altar, under its ledge.
Carrying poles are needed for the altar too. Cut them from acacia and sheathe them in bronze.
Slide the poles into the rings so that they lie along the altar’s two sides whenever it is lifted.
Build the altar as a hollow box out of planks. Do it exactly as you were shown on the mountain.
Make a courtyard around the dwelling. On the south side, the hangings are to be of finely spun linen, 150 feet long.{c}
They are held by twenty posts set in twenty bronze bases, with silver hooks and bands{d} on the posts.
The north side is to match: 150 feet of hangings, twenty posts, twenty bronze bases, and silver hooks and bands.
The west side is 75 feet wide,{e} with hangings, ten posts, and ten bases.
The east end, the front, is also 75 feet wide.
One side of the gate gets a stretch of hangings 22½ feet long,{f} held by three posts on three bases.
The same goes for the other side of the gate: 22½ feet of hangings, three posts, and three bases.
For the courtyard gate, weave a screen 30 feet wide,{g} using blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen, the work of an embroiderer. Four posts on four bases support it.
All the posts around the courtyard are to be joined by silver bands and have silver hooks and bronze bases.
The courtyard will measure 150 feet long and 75 feet wide,{h} with hangings of finely spun linen 7½ feet high,{i} on bronze bases.
All the other tools for the work in the dwelling, along with its tent pegs and those of the courtyard, are to be bronze.
Command the Israelites to bring you clear oil from pressed olives for the light, so a flame burns continually.

Aaron and his sons will look after the lamp in the Tent of Meeting,{j} outside the curtain that hides the chest of the tablets. They keep it lit before Yahweh from dusk to dawn. This is a permanent rule for the Israelites, for every generation.”

notes.text: Hebrew “five cubits long and five cubits wide … three cubits high.” On the cubit (18 inches), see the note at 25:10. In meters the altar was about 2.3 meters square and 1.4 meters high.
Projections shaped like horns at the corners of the altar, the holiest part of it (29:12).
Hebrew “a hundred cubits,” about 45 meters. So also in verse 11 and in verse 18.
Or “connecting rods.”
Hebrew “fifty cubits.” So also in verses 13 and 18.
Hebrew “fifteen cubits.” So also in verse 15.
Hebrew “twenty cubits.”
Hebrew “a hundred cubits long and fifty wide,” where verse 18 reads “fifty by fifty,” which may mean fifty cubits at each end.
Hebrew “five cubits.”
Hebrew ohel mo’ed, the tent where Yahweh met with Moses and the people (29:42–43). It is another name for the tabernacle.

verses.text: “Bring Aaron, your brother, forward from the Israelites, and his four sons with him: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. They are to be my priests.
Sew sacred garments for your brother Aaron, clothing that brings him dignity and splendor.
Speak to all the skilled workers I have gifted with ability.{a} They are to make Aaron’s clothes, to set him apart so that he can serve me as priest.

These are the garments they will make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash. They will make these holy garments for your brother Aaron and his sons, so that they may serve me as priests.
The workers are to use gold, and blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine linen.
The ephod is to be crafted by a skilled worker from gold, blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen.
It must have two shoulder pieces fastened to its two upper corners, to hold it together.
The woven waistband{b} on it is to match the ephod and be made of the same materials: gold, blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen.
Take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel,
Put six of the names on one stone and the other six on the second, arranged by age.
Cut the names of Israel’s sons into the two stones the way a gem cutter engraves a seal, and enclose them in gold settings.
Then fasten the stones onto the ephod’s shoulder pieces, as stones to remind God of Israel’s sons. Aaron is to bear these names on his shoulders in Yahweh’s presence, to bring them to mind.
Make gold settings,
and braid two chains from pure gold, twisting them like rope, and hook the chains to the settings.
Make a breastpiece for making decisions, the work of a skilled craftsman. Make it like the ephod, from gold and blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen.
The breastpiece is to be a square when folded double, with sides of 9 inches.{c}
Fix four rows of precious stones to it. Row one: carnelian, topaz, emerald.
Row two: turquoise, lapis lazuli,{d} and diamond.{e}
in the third row a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst;
and in the fourth row a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. Set each one in gold.
The twelve stones match the names of Israel’s sons, and each is engraved like a seal with the name of one tribe.
For the breastpiece, also twist chains of pure gold into a cord.
Make two gold rings and fasten them to two corners of the breastpiece.
Hook the pair of gold cords into the rings at the breastpiece’s corners,
and fasten the free ends of both chains to the two settings, linking them to the front of the ephod’s shoulder pieces.
Make two more gold rings and attach them to the two lower corners of the breastpiece, on the inside edge next to the ephod.
Make another two gold rings and fasten them low on the front of the ephod’s shoulder pieces, near the seam, above the woven waistband.
A blue cord must tie the breastpiece’s rings to the ephod’s rings, so that the breastpiece lies against the waistband and cannot slip off the ephod.
Whenever Aaron goes into the Holy Place, he will bear Israel’s sons’ names over his heart, engraved on the decision breastpiece, to keep them always in Yahweh’s mind.

Put the Urim and Thummim{f} in the breastpiece, so they rest over Aaron’s heart each time he comes before Yahweh. Over his heart, in Yahweh’s presence, Aaron will always carry the way Israel’s decisions are made.
Make the robe of the ephod entirely of blue cloth.
It must have an opening for the head in the middle, with a woven edge around it, like the collar of a coat,{g} so that it will not tear.
Around the hem make pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, with gold bells between them.
A gold bell, then a pomegranate, then a bell, then a pomegranate, goes all the way around the robe’s hem.
Aaron is to put it on each time he serves. Listeners will hear the bells as he goes into the Holy Place and as he leaves, and he will not die.
Make a gold plate, pure gold, and cut into it, as a seal is cut, the words HOLY TO YAHWEH.{h}
Tie it with blue cord to the turban, across the front.
It will rest on Aaron’s forehead. He is responsible for any fault in the sacred gifts that the Israelites dedicate. Because it is always on his forehead, Yahweh will accept the gifts.
The tunic, of fine linen, is to be woven in a checked pattern. A fine linen turban is needed too, and an embroidered sash.
For Aaron’s sons, make tunics, sashes, and caps that give them dignity and splendor.
Have Aaron and his sons put these on. Then anoint them, install them, and set them apart to be my priests.{i}
Also make them linen shorts to cover their bodies, from waist to thigh.

Aaron and his sons must wear them whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to serve in the Holy Place, so that they will not incur guilt and die. This is to be a lasting rule for Aaron and his descendants after him.”

notes.text: Hebrew “wise of heart.” The Hebrew word hokhmah, “wisdom,” here means practical skill.
Or “belt,” a belt woven as part of the ephod.
Hebrew “a span long and a span wide.” A span, the distance from thumb to little finger with the hand spread, was half a cubit, about 9 inches (23 centimeters).

Hebrew sappir. The ancient sapphire was probably lapis lazuli. The identification of several of these stones is uncertain, and the English names follow the Septuagint and modern proposals. Compare the stones of the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21:19–20.
Hebrew yahalom, perhaps a hard stone such as jasper or onyx. Diamonds were probably not cut in ancient Israel.

The Urim and Thummim were objects kept in the breastpiece and used to learn God’s will (Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 28:6). Their form and use are uncertain. The words may mean “lights and perfections,” or they may begin with the first and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet.
The meaning of the Hebrew word tahra is uncertain. It may mean a leather collar or the neck opening of a garment.
Hebrew tsits, “flower” or “shining thing,” perhaps a rosette-shaped plate.
Hebrew “fill their hand,” an expression for installing priests in office.

subheads.36: The turban plate and the other garments

verses.text: “Here is the procedure for setting Aaron and his sons apart as my priests. You will need a young bull and two rams, all without defect,
and bread, cakes mixed with oil, and thin wafers brushed with oil, all made without yeast from fine wheat flour.
Place these in a single basket and carry it forward, with the bull and the two rams.
Lead Aaron and his sons to the door of the Tent of Meeting, where you will bathe them in water.
Pick up the garments. Aaron gets the tunic first, then the ephod’s robe, the ephod, and the breastpiece. Bind the ephod to him using its woven waistband.
Set the turban on his head, and attach the holy crown{a} to it.
Then pour anointing oil over his head and so anoint him.
After that, his sons come forward, and you put tunics on them.
Tie sashes on Aaron and his sons and fit caps on their heads. By a lasting rule the priesthood is theirs. In this way you ordain Aaron and his sons.
Lead the bull up to the front of the Tent of Meeting, where Aaron and his sons will rest their hands on its head.
You will kill it before Yahweh, right at the door of the Tent of Meeting.
With your finger, put some of the blood on the altar’s horns, then pour the remaining blood out at the foot of the altar.
Take all the fat that covers the inner organs, the fatty part of the liver,{b} and both kidneys with their fat, and burn them on the altar.
The bull’s meat, hide, and waste must be burned outside the camp. It is a sin offering.{c}
Then take one of the rams. Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on its head.
Slaughter it, and splash its blood on all sides of the altar.
Cut the ram up, wash the entrails and legs, and set them beside the other parts and the head.
Burn the entire ram on the altar. It is a burnt offering to Yahweh, a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to Yahweh.
Then fetch the second ram. Aaron and his sons will press their hands against its head.

After you kill it, take a little of the blood and touch it to Aaron’s right earlobe, then to the right earlobes of his sons. Do the same to the right thumbs and the right big toes. The blood left over is to be thrown against the altar on every side.

Next, take a bit of blood from the altar, along with some anointing oil, and sprinkle both over Aaron and his garments, and over his sons and their garments. In this way he, his sons, and all their clothing become holy.
From this ram take the fat, the fat tail, the fat covering the inner organs, the fatty part of the liver, both kidneys with their fat, and the right thigh. (This is the ram for installing priests.)
From the basket of unleavened bread that sits in front of Yahweh, take a loaf, a cake made with oil, and a wafer.
Put each of these in the hands of Aaron and his sons, and have them raise the items before Yahweh as a presentation offering.{d}
Take the items back from them and burn them on the altar, over the burnt offering. This produces a pleasing aroma for Yahweh, an offering by fire.
Take the breast of the ram that installs Aaron, and lift it up before Yahweh as a presentation offering. That part will be yours.
Dedicate the parts of the installation ram that go to Aaron and his sons, that is, the breast that was lifted and the thigh that was held up.
This will always be the share that Aaron and his sons receive from the Israelites. It is a contribution from the people, taken from their fellowship offerings,{e} their gift to Yahweh.
Aaron’s holy garments will be passed on to his descendants, who will wear them when they are anointed and installed.
The son who succeeds Aaron as priest wears these clothes for a week, beginning the day he goes into the Tent of Meeting to minister inside the Holy Place.
Boil the meat of the installation ram in a holy place.
Aaron and his sons will eat that meat, together with the bread from the basket, at the door of the Tent of Meeting.
They alone may eat what was offered to atone for them and set them apart. An outsider cannot eat it, since it is holy.{f}
Should some of the meat or bread remain at dawn, burn it up. Nobody may eat it, for it is holy.
Do for Aaron and his sons exactly what I have ordered you, taking seven days to install them.
On each of the seven days, offer a bull as a sin offering for atonement. Purify the altar through atonement and pour oil on it to consecrate it.
Spend seven days in this way atoning for the altar and consecrating it. After that the altar will be especially holy, and anything that touches it becomes holy.
This is the daily routine for the altar, never to be skipped: two year-old lambs.
Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight.{g}
Along with the first lamb, present two quarts of fine flour{h} blended with a quart of pressed olive oil,{i} and a quart of wine poured out as a drink offering.
Offer the second lamb at twilight with the same grain offering and drink offering as in the morning. It is a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to Yahweh.
For all generations, this daily burnt offering must be presented at the door of the Tent of Meeting, before Yahweh. At that place I will meet with you and talk to you.
There I will also meet the Israelites, and my glory will make the place holy.
The Tent of Meeting and the altar I will make holy, and Aaron and his sons I will consecrate to be my priests.
I will live in the middle of the Israelites. I will be their God, and they will be my people.
They will understand that I, Yahweh, am their God, the one who rescued them from Egypt in order to live in their midst. I am Yahweh their God.”

notes.text: That is, the gold plate inscribed “Holy to Yahweh” (28:36).
Or “the appendage of the liver.” The exact organ is uncertain.
Hebrew hatta’t, also translated “purification offering.”
Hebrew tenufah, an offering presented by moving it toward the altar and back, or lifting it up.
Hebrew shelamim, also translated “peace offerings” or “offerings of well-being.”
Hebrew zar, a person not of the priestly family.
Hebrew “between the two evenings,” understood either as between sunset and dark or as between midafternoon and sunset. So also in verse 41.
Hebrew “a tenth,” meaning a tenth of an ephah, about 2.2 liters. An ephah was about 3/5 of a bushel.
Hebrew “a quarter of a hin,” about 0.9 liter. A hin was about 1 gallon (3.7 liters), though estimates of ancient liquid measures vary. The drink offering of wine in verse 40 was also a quarter hin.

subheads.10: The bull for the sin offering

verses.text: Build an altar of acacia wood to burn incense on.
It must be a square, 18 inches by 18 inches, standing 36 inches high,{a} with its horns forming one piece with the rest.
Cover the top surface, the four sides, and the horns in pure gold, and add a gold border around the rim.
Beneath the border, on two opposite sides, attach two gold rings. These will hold the carrying poles.
The poles are acacia wood, covered in gold.
Put the altar just outside the curtain that screens the chest of the tablets, directly in line with the cover over the tablets, which is where I will meet you.
Each morning, as he prepares the lamps, Aaron is to burn fragrant incense there.
He is to burn incense again at twilight, when he lights the lamps.{b} Incense is to be burned before Yahweh from one generation to the next.
Offer no unauthorized incense on this altar, and no burnt offering, grain offering, or drink offering.
Once a year Aaron is to make atonement on its horns. He will do it with the blood of the sin offering for atonement, every year for all generations. The altar is most holy to Yahweh.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“When you take a count of the Israelites, each man must pay Yahweh a ransom for his life as he is counted. That way no plague will strike them while they are being counted.
Everyone who is counted must give half a shekel, using the sanctuary’s standard.{c} That is about one fifth of an ounce of silver, given as a contribution to Yahweh.
Every person counted, from age twenty up, must give Yahweh this contribution.
When you bring this payment to Yahweh to atone for your lives, the wealthy must pay no more than half a shekel, and the poor no less.
Collect the atonement money from the Israelites and use it for the work of the Tent of Meeting. It will be a reminder of the Israelites before Yahweh, to atone for your lives.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
Make a washbasin of bronze, on a bronze base. Set it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, filled with water.
Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and feet in it.
When they go into the Tent of Meeting, or step up to the altar to burn an offering for Yahweh, they have to wash in water first, or they will die.
Hands and feet must be washed, or they will die. This rule is permanent for Aaron and his descendants, in every generation.”
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Gather the best spices available. You need liquid myrrh{d} weighing 12½ pounds, cinnamon and cane{e} weighing 6¼ pounds each,
and 12½ pounds of cassia,{f} all by the sanctuary’s standard,{g} together with a gallon of olive oil.{h}
Blend these ingredients, as a perfumer does, into a sacred anointing oil. That is what it will be.
With it, anoint the Tent of Meeting and the chest of the tablets,
the table with all it holds, the lampstand with everything that goes with it, the altar for incense,
the burnt offering altar with its equipment, and the washbasin with its base.
Set them apart, so that they are especially holy. Anything that touches them will be holy as well.
Anoint Aaron and his sons, and set them apart to serve me as priests.
Tell the Israelites, ‘This will be my holy anointing oil for all your generations.
Never pour it on an ordinary person,{i} and never copy the recipe to make oil of your own. It is sacred, so you are to regard it as sacred.
Whoever blends a perfume like it, or applies it to someone outside the priesthood, will be cut off from his people.’”
Yahweh told Moses, “Take fragrant spices, namely stacte, onycha, and galbanum,{j} along with pure frankincense. Use equal weights of each.
Make them into incense, blended like perfume, seasoned with salt, pure and holy.
Grind some of it into fine powder and put it in front of the chest of the tablets in the Tent of Meeting, where I will meet you. You are to treat it as most holy.
Do not make incense with this recipe for your own use. Treat it as holy to Yahweh.
Anyone who makes something like it to enjoy its fragrance will be cut off from his people.”

notes.text: Hebrew “a cubit long and a cubit wide … two cubits high.” On the cubit (18 inches), see the note at 25:10.
Hebrew “between the two evenings.” See the note at 12:6.

Hebrew “half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel is twenty gerahs),” about 5.7 grams. A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams) and a gerah one-twentieth of a shekel. The “sanctuary shekel” may have been a standard kept at the sanctuary, or a heavier shekel.
Hebrew “five hundred shekels,” about 5.75 kilograms. So also for the cassia in verse 24.

Hebrew “two hundred fifty shekels,” about 2.9 kilograms. So also for the cane in the same verse. The Hebrew for cane may also mean “calamus,” an aromatic reed. The identification of several of these spices is uncertain.
Hebrew qiddah, a spice from the bark of a plant related to cinnamon.
Hebrew “by the shekel of the sanctuary.” See the note at verse 13.
Hebrew “a hin of olive oil,” about 3.7 liters, or one gallon.
Hebrew “on the flesh of man,” that is, on ordinary people.
The identity of stacte (Hebrew nataf, “drops”), onycha (Hebrew shehelet, perhaps from a shellfish), and galbanum (a plant resin) is not certain.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Understand this: Bezalel,{a} Uri’s son and Hur’s grandson, from Judah’s tribe, is the man I have personally selected.
I have given him the Spirit of God, together with skill, understanding, knowledge, and ability in every sort of craft.
He can plan artistic designs and work in gold, silver, and bronze,
cut and set gemstones, and carve wood. He is able to work in every craft.
Beside him I have placed Oholiab,{b} the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. I have also given talent to every other skilled worker, so that they can build all that I ordered you to have made:
the Tent of Meeting, the chest of the tablets with the cover over it, and all the tent’s other furnishings,
the table and its equipment, the pure gold lampstand and every tool for it, the altar of incense,
the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, the basin with its stand,
the beautifully woven garments,{c} the sacred garments for Aaron the priest, and the clothing his sons wear for their priestly service,
the anointing oil, and the sweet incense used in the Holy Place. They are to make all of it just as I have directed you.”
Yahweh gave Moses another message:
“Speak to the Israelites: ‘You must keep my Sabbaths. For every generation, the Sabbath is a sign between me and you, so that you will know that I am Yahweh, the one who makes you holy.{d}
Honor the Sabbath day, for it belongs to you as something holy. Whoever profanes it is to be executed, and anyone who does work then will be cut off from the people.
Six days are for working, but the seventh is a day of total rest,{e} holy to Yahweh. Whoever works on the Sabbath day is to be executed.
The Israelites are to observe the Sabbath, honoring it in every generation as a lasting covenant.
It is a permanent sign between me and the Israelites. Yahweh made heaven and earth over six days, and on the seventh he ceased his work and rested.’”
When Yahweh finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, he gave him the two tablets of the covenant, stone tablets written by the finger of God.

notes.text: Bezalel means “in the shadow (protection) of God.”
Oholiab means “the father is my tent.”
Or “the woven,” or “the service.” The meaning of the Hebrew word serad is uncertain.
Hebrew YHWH meqaddishkem, “Yahweh who sanctifies you.” Compare Leviticus 20:8.
Hebrew shabbat shabbaton, “a Sabbath of Sabbath rest.”

verses.text: The people saw that Moses was staying on the mountain far too long. So they gathered around Aaron and said, “Come on, make us gods{a} that will march ahead of us. That Moses, the one who led us out of Egypt, has vanished, and nobody knows his fate.”
Aaron told them, “Pull off the gold rings hanging from the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them here.”
So all the people took the gold rings out of their ears and carried them to Aaron.
Aaron took what they handed him, formed it with a carving tool,{b} and cast a calf-shaped idol. The people cried out, “Here are your gods, Israel! They are the ones that rescued you from Egypt!”
Aaron noticed their excitement. He set up an altar in front of the calf and called out, “Tomorrow there will be a festival for Yahweh!”
At dawn the next day the people presented burnt offerings and fellowship offerings. They settled down to a meal with plenty to drink, and then they got up to celebrate wildly.{c}
Yahweh spoke to Moses: “Hurry down the mountain! The people you led out of Egypt have become depraved.

It did not take them long to wander from the road I told them to follow. They have cast a metal calf, they bow before it, they sacrifice to it, and they declare, ‘Israel, these are your gods, who rescued you from Egypt.’”
Yahweh added, “I have taken a good look at this nation. They are a hardheaded, stubborn people.
So step aside and let my fury burn against them until it consumes them. Afterward I will make you the ancestor of a great nation.”
But Moses pleaded with Yahweh his God. “Yahweh,” he said, “why should your anger blaze against your own people, whom you rescued from Egypt with tremendous power and a strong hand?

Why should the Egyptians have the chance to say, ‘He led them out with evil in mind. His plan was to slaughter them in the mountains and erase them from the earth’? Let go of your fierce anger and change your mind.{d} Spare your people from this calamity.

Think about the promise you gave Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, who served you. You vowed by your own name, ‘Your descendants will be as numerous as the stars in the sky, and this entire land I promised will be theirs for all time.’”
So Yahweh changed his mind, and the calamity he had threatened never fell on his people.
Moses went back down from the mountain, holding the two tablets of the covenant. Writing covered both of their faces, front and back.
The tablets were God’s own handiwork. The words carved into them were his own writing.
Joshua heard the people yelling and said to Moses, “That sounds like fighting down in the camp.”

Moses replied, “That is not the sound of men cheering a victory,
and it is not the wailing of men who were beaten.
I hear the sound of singing.{e}”
As Moses drew near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, he boiled with rage. He flung the tablets from his hands and they shattered at the foot of the mountain.
Next he grabbed the calf they had cast, burned it up, and ground it down to powder. He sprinkled the powder over the water and made the Israelites drink the mixture.
Moses said to Aaron, “How did this people harm you? Why did you drag them into such a great sin?”
“Please don’t be angry, my lord,” Aaron answered. “You know how these people are, always set on doing wrong.
They said to me, ‘Make gods to march in front of us. That Moses, who led us out of Egypt, has disappeared, and we don’t know his fate.’
So I told them, ‘Anyone with gold jewelry should take it off.’ They gave it to me, I tossed it into the fire, and out came this calf!”
Moses saw that the people were out of control. Aaron had let them run wild, and their enemies would now laugh at them.
So Moses took his stand at the entrance to the camp and called out, “Anyone who is on Yahweh’s side, come here to me!” All the Levites rallied to him.

He said to them, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, commands this: ‘Each of you must strap on a sword, then march through the camp from one entrance to the other, striking down your own brothers, friends, and neighbors.’”
The Levites did what Moses told them, and roughly three thousand of the people fell dead before the day ended.
Moses said to them, “This day you have been ordained{f} to serve Yahweh, because each of you opposed a son or a brother. So he now grants you his blessing.”
Morning came, and Moses addressed the people. “Your sin is monstrous,” he said. “I am going back up to Yahweh. Perhaps I will be able to win forgiveness for you.”
So Moses went back to Yahweh and said, “Oh, how terrible! These people have committed an enormous sin. They have made themselves gods of gold.
Forgive them, I beg you! Yet if you refuse, wipe my name out of the book you have been writing.”
Yahweh answered Moses, “Anyone who has sinned against me is the one I will wipe out of my book.
You must leave now and guide the people toward the land I described. My angel will lead the way. Even so, on the day I come to call them to account, their sin will be punished.”
And Yahweh struck the people with a plague because of the calf that Aaron had made.

notes.text: Or “a god.” Hebrew elohim with a plural verb; the same form is used in verses 4, 8, and 23. Compare 1 Kings 12:28.
Or “tied it up in a bag.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew verb tsahaq can include revelry or sexual play. Compare 1 Corinthians 10:7.
Or “change your mind.” Hebrew niham, used also in verse 14.
Hebrew “of answering,” perhaps singing in response, or antiphonal singing. The Septuagint reads “of those who begin a song over wine.”
Hebrew “Fill your hands,” the expression for ordination to priestly service (28:41). The Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint, and Vulgate read, “You have ordained yourselves.”

verses.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Move on from here, you and the people you rescued from Egypt. The land I vowed to give Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is your destination. I told them, ‘It will belong to your descendants.’
An angel will go in front of you, and he will expel the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
The land you are heading for is rich and fertile, flowing with milk and honey. But I won’t be traveling in your midst. You are too hardheaded, and I could destroy you on the road.”
The people were crushed when they heard these harsh words, and they went into mourning. No one wore any ornaments.

Yahweh had instructed Moses, “Tell the Israelites: ‘You are hardheaded. One moment in your company would be enough for me to wipe you out. Now remove your ornaments, and I will figure out how to deal with you.’”
So the Israelites stripped themselves of their ornaments at Mount Horeb and did not wear them again.
Moses had a habit of pitching a tent{a} well away from the camp. He named it the tent of meeting. Whoever needed to seek Yahweh’s guidance walked out to it, beyond the edge of the camp.
Whenever Moses headed for the tent, the people all stood, each at the entrance of his own tent, and kept their eyes on Moses until he disappeared inside.
Once Moses was inside, the pillar of cloud descended and hovered at the entrance, and Yahweh{b} talked with Moses.
When the people saw the pillar of cloud hovering there, they all stood up and bowed down, each at his own tent entrance.

Yahweh talked with Moses face to face, the way two friends talk. When the conversation was over, Moses returned to the camp, but his attendant, a young man named Joshua son of Nun,{c} stayed in the tent.
Moses told Yahweh, “You order me to lead this people, but you have not said who will go along with me. You told me you know me by name and that I have won your favor.
If that is true, show me your ways. Then I will know you, and I can go on enjoying your favor. Keep in mind that these people belong to you.”
Yahweh replied, “My presence{d} will accompany you, and you will have rest.”
Moses told him, “Unless your presence goes with us, don’t send us out of here.
Otherwise, how could anyone tell that you are pleased with me and your people? Your going with us is what makes us different, me and your people, from all the peoples on earth.”
Yahweh told Moses, “I will grant this request too. You have won my favor, and I know you by name.”
Moses said, “Then please, let me see your glory!”

Yahweh answered, “I will let all my goodness go by you, and I will speak my name,{e} Yahweh, as it goes. Mercy is for the people I choose to pity, and compassion is for those I choose to treat tenderly.{f}
But my face you cannot look at, because no human can see me and survive.”
Yahweh said, “Look, there is a place close to me. Stand on the rock there.
As my glory moves past, I will tuck you into a crevice in the rock and hold my hand over you until I have passed.
Then I will take away my hand, and you can look at my back.{g} My face, though, must remain unseen.”

notes.text: Here the “tent of meeting” is a tent pitched outside the camp before the tabernacle was built (compare chapters 35–40).
Hebrew “he.”
Joshua is called “son of Nun” here for the first time. Nun means “fish.”
Hebrew “my face,” so also in verse 15 (“your face”). The Septuagint reads “I myself will go before you.”
Or “I will call out the name ‘Yahweh’ in front of you.” See 34:5–7.
Paul quotes these words in Romans 9:15.
Or “my aftermath,” what remains after I have passed. The Hebrew is unusual and the language is deliberately reserved.

subheads.1: Yahweh refuses to go with them
subheads.12: Moses asks to see Yahweh’s glory

verses.text: Yahweh told Moses, “Carve out a new pair of stone tablets, just like the first. On them I will inscribe the words that were on the first pair, which you broke.
Be ready by morning and climb Mount Sinai. Stand before me there on the mountaintop.
Nobody may go up with you or even show up anywhere on the mountain. Not even the sheep and cattle may graze near it.”
Moses carved out a new pair of stone tablets like the originals. At dawn he climbed Mount Sinai, just as Yahweh had directed, and he carried the tablets with him.
Yahweh came down in the cloud and stood with him there and called out his name, Yahweh.{a}
Yahweh passed in front of Moses and called out,{b} “Yahweh, Yahweh, God of compassion{c} and grace, patient, rich in loyal love{d} and truth,{e}

showing loyal love to a thousand generations,{f} forgiving guilt, rebellion, and sin. But he does not simply excuse the guilty. He holds children and grandchildren responsible for their parents’ sin, down to the third and fourth generation.”
Moses quickly bent down to the ground and worshiped.
He said, “My Lord,{g} if I have truly won your favor, please travel with us. These are a stubborn people, yes. But forgive our guilt and sin, and make us your own possession.”

Yahweh declared, “Here is my covenant: before all your people I will do wonders that no nation anywhere has ever witnessed. Everyone around you will see Yahweh’s work. What I will accomplish through you is awe-inspiring.
Obey my orders for today. Ahead of you I will expel the Amorites, Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
Take care that you never make a treaty with the people living in the land you are entering. That would become a trap for you.
No, you are to demolish their altars, break their sacred pillars into pieces, and cut down their Asherah poles.{h}
You must never bow to any other god, because Yahweh, whose name is Jealous,{i} is a God who tolerates no rivals.

Do not make a treaty with the people of that land. They give themselves like prostitutes to their gods and offer sacrifices to them. If you made a treaty, they would invite you, and you would end up eating their sacrificial meals.
You might even take their daughters as wives for your sons. Then those daughters, giving themselves like prostitutes to their gods, would lead your sons to do the same.
Never make gods of cast metal for yourselves.
Observe the Festival of Unleavened Bread. Eat bread without yeast through seven days, as I ordered you. Hold it at the appointed time during Abib,{j} for in that month you walked out of Egypt.
Every firstborn male belongs to me.{k} That includes the firstborn of all your livestock, both cattle and sheep.
A firstborn donkey can be redeemed with a lamb. If you won’t redeem it, then snap its neck. Every firstborn son must be redeemed too. Do not show up in my presence empty-handed.
Six days are for your labor; on the seventh, stop. Stop even in the plowing season and the harvest season.
Keep the Festival of Weeks{l} when you bring the first of the wheat harvest. Keep the Festival of Ingathering when the year comes to its end.
Three times a year every man among you is to present himself to the Lord Yahweh,{m} Israel’s God.
I will drive nations away from you and expand your territory. While you go up to appear before Yahweh your God three times a year, no one will covet your land.
Never offer the blood of a sacrifice to me together with anything made with yeast. And never leave any of the Passover festival sacrifice until morning.
Bring the very best of the first harvest from your land to the house of Yahweh your God. Never boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.{n}”
Yahweh then told Moses, “Write down what I have just said. These words are the basis of the covenant I now make with you and with Israel.”
Moses stayed on the mountain with Yahweh forty days and nights. He had no bread and no water. And the terms of the covenant, the Ten Words,{p} were written on the tablets by him.{o}
Moses went down Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the covenant. He had no idea that his skin was glowing{q} from his conversation with Yahweh.{r}
Aaron and the whole nation of Israel looked at Moses, and his face was glowing. They were too frightened to approach.
Moses called out to them, though. Aaron and all the community leaders returned, and Moses addressed them.
Later the rest of the Israelites came closer, and Moses relayed all the instructions Yahweh had given him on Mount Sinai.
When he had finished delivering them, Moses draped a veil over his face.

But any time Moses entered Yahweh’s presence to speak with him, he took the veil off, and he left it off until he came out. Once outside, he would relay to the Israelites whatever instructions he had received.
The people could see Moses’ shining face. Afterward he would cover it again with the veil, until the next time he entered to talk with Yahweh.

notes.text: Or “he called on the name of Yahweh.” The subject may be Yahweh or Moses.

These words (verses 6–7) are Yahweh’s own declaration of his character, the fullest self-description in the Old Testament. They are echoed again and again: Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalms 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Nahum 1:3. Grammatically the first words may also be read, “Yahweh, Yahweh is a God compassionate….”
Hebrew el rahum vehannun. Rahum, “compassionate,” is related to rehem, “womb,” suggesting a mother’s tender love; hannun, “gracious,” describes favor freely given.
Hebrew hesed, the loyal, committed love that keeps covenant. See the note at 15:13.
Hebrew emet, “truth,” “reliability,” “faithfulness.”
Or “to the thousandth generation” (compare Deuteronomy 7:9). The contrast with “the third and the fourth generation” stresses that God’s mercy far outweighs his judgment.
Hebrew Adonai, “my Lord.” Some Hebrew manuscripts read “Yahweh.”
Hebrew asherim, wooden poles or images associated with the goddess Asherah.
Hebrew Qanna. On God’s jealousy, see the note at 20:5. Here “Jealous” is presented as a name, expressing his exclusive claim on his people.
Hebrew “the month of Abib.” See the note at 13:4.
Hebrew “everything that opens the womb.”
Hebrew shavu’ot, later called Pentecost (“fiftieth”), because it came seven weeks (fifty days) after Passover.
Hebrew ha’adon YHWH elohe yisra’el, “the Lord Yahweh, the God of Israel.” On ha’adon see the note at 23:17.
See the note at 23:19.
The context suggests that Yahweh is the one who wrote (verse 1; Deuteronomy 10:2–4), though grammatically the subject could be Moses (verse 27).
Hebrew “the ten words,” the source of the term “Decalogue.” Compare Deuteronomy 4:13; 10:4.

Hebrew qaran, related to qeren, “horn.” The verb probably means “sent out rays.” The Latin Vulgate rendered it cornuta, “horned,” which led to medieval and Renaissance art (including Michelangelo’s statue) showing Moses with horns. The Septuagint reads “was glorified.”
That is, with Yahweh.

subheads.8: Moses’ prayer and the covenant renewed

verses.text: Moses assembled the entire Israelite community and told them, “Yahweh has given these orders, and you are to carry them out.{a}
You have six days to work. The seventh day is holy to you, a Sabbath of total rest in Yahweh’s honor. Death is the penalty for anyone who works on that day.
On the Sabbath you may not light a fire in any place where you live.”
Moses then told the whole community of Israel, “Here is what Yahweh has ordered.
Set aside a gift for Yahweh from your own belongings. Let everyone with a generous heart bring it: gold, silver, and bronze,
blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, fine linen, and goat hair,
ram skins dyed red, fine leather, and acacia wood,
olive oil for the lamps, and spices for making the anointing oil and the fragrant incense,
and gems, including onyx, to be fixed on the ephod and the breastpiece.
Every skilled worker among you should step forward and build everything Yahweh has ordered:
the dwelling itself: its bases, frames, crossbars, posts, clasps, tent, and covering;
the chest with its carrying poles, the cover, and the curtain that hides the chest from view;
the table with poles, dishes, and other equipment, plus the bread of the Presence;
the lampstand that provides light, together with its tools, its lamps, and the lamp oil;
the incense altar and poles, the anointing oil, the fragrant incense, and the screen at the dwelling’s entrance;
the altar of burnt offering, with its bronze grate, poles, and utensils, and the washbasin and its stand;
the courtyard hangings, with their posts and bases, and the screen for the courtyard’s gate;
the tent pegs and ropes for the dwelling and the courtyard;
and the finely woven garments for service in the sanctuary, including the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the clothing for his sons.”
With that, the entire Israelite community left Moses.
Everyone who felt inspired and willing came and gave to Yahweh. The gifts went toward building the tent of meeting, equipping it for service, and making the holy garments.

Men and women alike, everyone with a willing heart, came forward. They brought gold items of every kind: pins, earrings, signet rings, and necklaces.{b} Each one lifted up a gold gift and presented it to Yahweh.
Everyone who owned blue, purple, or scarlet yarn, fine linen, goat hair, red-dyed ram skins, or fine leather brought it.
Those who could spare silver or bronze brought it to Yahweh as their gift. Anyone who owned acacia wood useful for the project brought that as well.
All the women with skill spun thread by hand, then brought the finished yarn in blue, purple, and scarlet, and the fine linen.
Every woman with the skill and the willingness to use it also spun the goat hair.
The leaders supplied onyx and other gems to be fixed on the ephod and the breastpiece,
as well as the spices and the oil for the lamps, the anointing oil, and the fragrant incense.
So the Israelites, every man and woman who felt moved to give, brought freewill gifts to Yahweh for all the work that Yahweh had commanded through Moses.
Moses then told the Israelites, “Look, Yahweh has personally chosen Bezalel from the tribe of Judah. He is the son of Uri and grandson of Hur.
He has filled Bezalel with the Spirit of God, with skill, understanding, and knowledge for every kind of work,
including the design of artistic pieces in gold, silver, and bronze,
the cutting and setting of gems, and the carving of wood. He can do any kind of artistic work.
Yahweh has given both Bezalel and Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan, the gift of teaching others.

He has filled them both with the skill to do every kind of work, whether as engravers or designers, as embroiderers in blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen, or as weavers. They can do every kind of work, and they can create original designs.”

notes.text: Chapters 35–40 report how the instructions of chapters 25–31 were carried out, repeating them almost word for word. In the Septuagint these chapters are shorter and arranged in a different order: for example, the priestly garments (Hebrew 39) come before the tabernacle structure (Hebrew 36), the making of the incense altar (Hebrew 37:25–28) is not reported, and several sections are abbreviated. In Brenton’s English edition the chapters are numbered differently, so that the curtains appear in chapter 37 and the ark in chapter 38. Scholars debate whether the Greek translator abridged and rearranged the Hebrew or worked from a different Hebrew edition. This translation follows the Hebrew order.
Or “pendants.” The identity of some of these ornaments is uncertain.

subheads.1: Sabbath rules and gifts for the sanctuary

verses.text: Bezalel, Oholiab, and all the skilled workers whom Yahweh had gifted with the know-how to build the sanctuary were to do the work exactly as Yahweh had commanded.
Moses summoned Bezalel, Oholiab, and every talented person whom Yahweh had equipped, everyone who felt eager to take part in the work.
They collected from Moses all the gifts the Israelites had brought for building the sanctuary. Yet each morning the people kept bringing more freewill gifts.
Finally all the skilled workers who were busy on the sanctuary stopped what they were doing,
and reported, “These people keep bringing us far more than the work Yahweh ordered requires.”
Moses sent out an order, and it was shouted throughout the camp: “Men and women, stop preparing contributions for the sanctuary!” So the people were held back from giving.
What they had already supplied was more than enough to finish every part of the work.

The skilled men among the workers made the dwelling first. Ten curtains went into it, woven from linen thread twisted fine and from wool dyed blue, purple, and scarlet, and a master craftsman worked winged creatures into the fabric.
Each curtain was the same size, about 42 feet long and 6 feet wide.{a}
He{b} stitched five of the curtains together into one set, and he did the same with the other five.
He sewed loops of blue cloth along the outer edge of the final curtain in one set, and did the same on the final curtain of the other set.
There were fifty loops on one curtain and fifty on the end curtain of the other set, placed so each loop faced another.
Next he made fifty gold clasps. With these he coupled the two sets, so that the dwelling formed a single unit.
