Next he made curtains of goat hair to serve as a tent over the dwelling. He made eleven of them.
All eleven were the same size, about 45 feet long and 6 feet wide.{c}
He joined five of them into one set and the other six into a second set.
He made fifty loops on the outer edge of the end curtain of the first set, and fifty more on the end curtain of the second.
Then he made fifty bronze clasps to connect the tent so that it formed one whole.
He made a cover for the tent from ram skins dyed red, and above it a cover of fine leather.
He built the upright frames for the dwelling from acacia wood.
Each frame stood 15 feet high and was 27 inches wide.{d}
Each had two projections set side by side. He built all the frames in this way.
The south side of the dwelling received twenty frames,
and under them he placed forty silver bases, two beneath each frame, one for each projection.
For the second side, the north, he also made twenty frames
and forty silver bases, with two under every frame.
The back of the dwelling, facing west, got six frames,
and two more for the corners at the back.
These corner frames were double thickness at the base and were joined at the top by one ring. Both corners were made this way.
In all there were eight frames, resting on sixteen silver bases, two under each frame.
Then he cut crossbars from acacia: five to tie together the frames along one side of the dwelling,
five for the frames along the opposite side, and five for those at the west end.
He made the middle crossbar run through the center of the frames from one end to the other.
The frames were covered with gold, and he made gold rings to hold the crossbars. The crossbars were covered with gold too.
He made the inner curtain from blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen, with winged creatures worked into it by a master craftsman.
For it he made four acacia posts and covered them with gold, with gold hooks, and he cast four silver bases for them.
At the entrance to the tent he hung a screen woven of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely twisted linen, an embroiderer’s work,
along with five posts and their hooks. He covered the tops of the posts and their connecting bands with gold, and he made their five bases of bronze.

notes.text: Hebrew “twenty-eight cubits” and “four cubits,” about 12.6 by 1.8 meters. A cubit was about 18 inches (45 centimeters); see the note at 25:10.
That is, Bezalel (37:1), with those who worked under him.
Hebrew “thirty cubits” and “four cubits,” about 13.5 by 1.8 meters.
Hebrew “ten cubits” and “a cubit and a half,” about 4.5 by 0.7 meters.

subheads.35: The inner curtain and the entrance screen

verses.text: Bezalel started with the chest, building it of acacia wood. Its measurements were 45 inches by 27 inches, with a height of 27 inches.{a}
Pure gold covered it, inside and out, and a gold border encircled its top edge.
He cast four gold rings for its feet and attached them, two on one side and two on the other.
Then he cut poles from acacia wood and covered them in gold.
The poles went through the rings on the sides of the chest, so that it could be carried.
The cover was a slab of pure gold measuring 45 inches by 27 inches.{b}
From gold he hammered two winged creatures and placed them at the two ends of the cover.
One creature was on the one end and one on the other. He shaped them from the same piece of gold as the cover itself.
Their wings were spread upward and shaded the cover. They faced one another, with their eyes turned toward the cover.
Next came the table, built of acacia wood. It measured 36 inches in length and 18 inches in width, and stood 27 inches tall.{c}
He covered it in pure gold and set a gold border around its edge.
He also fitted a rim about 3 inches wide{d} around the table and put a gold border along the rim.
He cast four gold rings and fastened them at the four corners, where the legs met the top.
The rings sat right next to the rim, and the carrying poles slid through them.
Those poles, used for lifting the table, were cut from acacia and plated with gold.
He made all the table’s accessories of pure gold: plates, dishes, jars, and the bowls used to pour out drink offerings.
He hammered the lampstand out of pure gold. Its base and shaft, its cups, and its buds and flowers formed a single piece with it.
Six branches came out of its sides, three from one side and three from the other.
Each of the six branches carried three cups shaped like almond flowers, each cup with its bud and blossom.
On the shaft of the lampstand itself were four cups shaped like almond flowers, each with its bud and blossom.
One bud was placed under the first pair of branches, another under the second pair, and another under the third pair, for all six branches.
The buds and branches were one piece with the lampstand, all hammered out of a single block of pure gold.
He also made its seven lamps, together with its wick trimmers and trays, all of pure gold.
He used about 75 pounds of pure gold{e} for the lampstand and all its accessories.
He built the incense altar from acacia wood. It was a square, 18 inches on each side and 36 inches high.{f} Its horns were made as one piece with the altar.
He plated the top, the sides, and the horns in pure gold, and he added a gold border around it.
Under the border he fastened two gold rings on opposite sides, to hold the poles used for carrying it.
The poles were acacia wood covered with gold.
He also prepared the holy anointing oil and the pure, fragrant incense, as a perfumer would.

notes.text: Hebrew “two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high,” about 1.1 by 0.7 by 0.7 meters. A cubit was about 18 inches (45 centimeters); see the note at 25:10.
Hebrew “two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide,” about 1.1 by 0.7 meters.
Hebrew “two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high,” about 90 by 45 by 70 centimeters.
Hebrew “a handbreadth,” about 3 inches (7.5 centimeters).
Hebrew “a talent of pure gold,” about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).
Hebrew “a cubit long and a cubit wide … two cubits high,” about 45 centimeters square and 90 centimeters high.

verses.text: Bezalel constructed the altar for burnt offerings from acacia wood. It was a square, 7½ feet on each side and 4½ feet high.{a}
At each of its four corners he made a horn, forming the horns out of the same piece as the altar, and he covered the whole thing with bronze.
He also made all the altar’s equipment of bronze: the pots, shovels, sprinkling bowls, meat forks, and fire pans.
For the altar he made a grate of bronze mesh and placed it beneath the ledge, halfway up from the ground.
He cast four bronze rings for the corners of the grate, to hold the carrying poles.
The poles were cut from acacia, and he plated them with bronze.
He slid the poles through the rings on the altar’s sides to carry it. The altar was hollow, built out of planks.
He made the bronze washbasin, with its bronze stand, from the mirrors{b} of the women who served{c} at the entrance to the tent of meeting.
Then he turned to the courtyard. Along the southern edge ran hangings of finely twisted linen, 150 feet in length.{d}
Twenty posts stood on twenty bronze bases to support them, and the posts carried silver hooks and bands.
The northern edge matched it, 150 feet of hangings supported by twenty posts on twenty bronze bases, with hooks and bands of silver.
Across the west end the hangings spanned 75 feet.{e} Ten posts and ten bases held them, again with silver hooks and bands.
The east end, which faced the sunrise, had the same width of 75 feet.
On one side of the gate the hangings stretched 22½ feet,{f} supported by three posts and three bases.
The opposite side of the gate was identical, with 22½ feet of hangings held by three posts on three bases.
Every hanging that enclosed the courtyard was made of finely twisted linen.
The bases for the posts were bronze, while the hooks and bands were silver. The tops of the posts were covered in silver, and all the courtyard posts were joined with silver bands.

The screen across the courtyard gate was an embroiderer’s work, of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn with finely twisted linen. It stretched 30 feet{g} and stood 7½ feet high,{h} the same height as the courtyard hangings.
Four posts on four bronze bases held it up. Silver hooks and bands were used, and the post tops were plated with silver.
Bronze was used for every tent peg of the dwelling and of the courtyard surrounding it.

This is the record{i} of the materials{j} used for the dwelling, the dwelling of the covenant tablets. At Moses’ command the Levites counted them, under the direction of Ithamar son of Aaron the priest.
Everything that Yahweh had ordered Moses to have made was built by Bezalel, Uri’s son and Hur’s grandson, of Judah’s tribe.
With him worked Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach of Dan’s tribe, a craftsman and designer who also did embroidery in blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen.
The gold that was contributed for all the work on the sanctuary totaled about 2,200 pounds,{k} weighed by the sanctuary standard.
The silver came from the men of the community who had been registered in the census, and it amounted to about 7,540 pounds,{l} weighed by the sanctuary standard.
That was a beka per person, half a shekel,{m} by the sanctuary standard, collected from each of the 603,550 men aged twenty and older who were counted.
The 7,500 pounds{n} of silver went into casting bases, a hundred in all, 75 pounds apiece, for the sanctuary wall and the inner curtain.
From the remaining 44 pounds{o} of silver he made the hooks for the posts, covered the tops of the posts, and made the connecting bands.
The bronze that was contributed came to about 5,300 pounds.{p}
With it he cast the bases at the entrance of the tent of meeting, the bronze altar with its grate and all its equipment,
the bases around the courtyard and at its gate, and all the tent pegs for the dwelling and the courtyard.

notes.text: Hebrew “five cubits long and five cubits wide … three cubits high,” about 2.3 meters square and 1.4 meters high.
Ancient mirrors were made of polished bronze.

Hebrew tsava’, used of organized service, including Levitical service at the sanctuary (Numbers 4:23; 8:24). Compare 1 Samuel 2:22. The nature of these women’s service is not explained. The Septuagint reads “of the women who fasted.”
Hebrew “a hundred cubits,” about 45 meters. So also in verse 11.
Hebrew “fifty cubits,” about 23 meters. So also in verse 13.
Hebrew “fifteen cubits,” about 6.8 meters. So also in verse 15.
Hebrew “twenty cubits,” about 9 meters.
Hebrew “five cubits,” about 2.3 meters.
Or “the inventory.”
Verses 21–31 are an accounting of the materials. In the Septuagint, this material appears in a different place and form (see the note at 35:1).

Hebrew “twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels,” about 1,000 kilograms. A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms) and a shekel about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams); a talent was 3,000 shekels. Standards varied, so these figures are approximate. On the “sanctuary standard” (Hebrew “shekel of the sanctuary”), see the note at 30:13. Some Septuagint manuscripts read 720 shekels.
Hebrew “a hundred talents and one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels,” about 3,400 kilograms.
Hebrew “a beka a head, half a shekel,” about 5.7 grams, or 0.2 ounce. The 603,550 contributors match the census in Numbers 1:46.
Hebrew “the hundred talents,” about 3,400 kilograms, that is, one talent (about 75 pounds or 34 kilograms) for each base.
Hebrew “one thousand seven hundred seventy-five shekels,” about 20 kilograms.
Hebrew “seventy talents and two thousand four hundred shekels,” about 2,400 kilograms.

verses.text: Using blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, the workers wove the finely made garments for service in the Holy Place. They also made the holy garments for Aaron, exactly as Yahweh had commanded Moses.
The ephod was made of gold thread, blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely twisted linen.

To prepare the gold thread, they hammered the metal into thin sheets and cut the sheets into strands. Skilled designers then worked the strands in with the blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and the linen.
They attached shoulder pieces to the ephod, fastening them at its two upper corners.
The woven waistband was made of the same materials and in the same style, with gold, blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and finely twisted linen, as Yahweh had commanded Moses.
The onyx stones were mounted in gold settings and engraved the way a seal is engraved, with the names of Israel’s sons.
Moses’ workers fastened the stones to the shoulder pieces of the ephod, to be reminders before God of Israel’s sons, as Yahweh had commanded Moses.
Next they made the breastpiece, a designer’s masterwork patterned after the ephod, using gold, blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely twisted linen.
It was square. They doubled it over, so that it measured 9 inches in each direction.{a}
On it they mounted gems in four rows. In row one were carnelian, topaz, and emerald;{b}
the second held turquoise, lapis lazuli, and diamond;
the third held jacinth, agate, and amethyst;
and the fourth held beryl, onyx, and jasper. Each stone was surrounded by a gold setting.
There were twelve stones, one for each of Israel’s sons. Each was engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes.
For the breastpiece they made chains of pure gold, braided like rope.
Two settings of gold and two rings of gold were crafted. The rings went on the top corners of the breastpiece.
The two braided gold chains were threaded through the rings at those corners.
The other ends of the chains were fastened to the two settings, which were fixed to the front of the ephod’s shoulder pieces.
Two further gold rings went on the lower corners of the breastpiece, on its inner edge facing the ephod.
They made yet another pair of gold rings and fixed them to the front of the ephod’s shoulder pieces, low down near the seam, above the woven waistband.
A blue cord tied the breastpiece’s rings to the ephod’s rings. This held the breastpiece above the woven waistband and kept it from sliding off the ephod, as Yahweh had commanded Moses.
The robe that goes under the ephod was woven entirely from blue yarn.
Its neck opening was in the center, with a woven binding around it, like the collar of a coat of armor,{c} to keep it from tearing.
For the lower edge of the robe they made pomegranates from blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine twisted linen.
Between the pomegranates, all around the hem, they hung bells of pure gold.
The pattern was a bell, then a pomegranate, over and over around the robe’s hem, to be worn for service, as Yahweh had commanded Moses.
For Aaron and his sons they wove tunics of fine linen,
and made the turban, the decorated caps, and the underwear, all of fine linen,
as well as the sash, which was embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn on twisted linen, as Yahweh had commanded Moses.
Then they made the sacred headband, a plate of pure gold, and carved the words HOLY TO YAHWEH into it as a seal is carved.
They attached a blue cord to it, to fasten it onto the front of the turban, as Yahweh had commanded Moses.
With that, all the work on the dwelling, the tent of meeting, was done. The Israelites carried out every detail of what Yahweh had commanded Moses.
They presented the dwelling to Moses. This included the tent and all its equipment, with the clasps, frames, crossbars, posts, and bases;
the covering of red-dyed ram skins, the covering of fine leather, and the curtain that screens the chest;
the chest of the tablets, its poles, and the cover;
the table, its equipment, and the bread of the Presence;
the pure gold lampstand with its row of lamps, all its tools, and the lamp oil;
the gold altar, the anointing oil, the sweet incense, and the screen at the entrance of the tent;
the bronze altar with its bronze grate, poles, and utensils, and the washbasin with its stand;
the courtyard hangings with their posts and bases, the screen for the courtyard gate with its ropes and pegs, and all the equipment for the service of the dwelling, the tent of meeting;
and the finely woven garments for service in the Holy Place, the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the clothing for his sons to wear when serving as priests.
The Israelites had finished all the work in the way Yahweh had commanded Moses.
Moses examined the whole project. They had done it all exactly as Yahweh had ordered. Moses then gave them his blessing.{d}

notes.text: Hebrew “a span long and a span wide,” about 23 centimeters square. See the note at 28:16.
On the identification of these stones, see the notes at 28:17–18.
See the note at 28:32.
The completion and blessing echo the end of the creation account: compare Genesis 1:31–2:3.

verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and said,
“On the first day of the first month,{a} you are to set up the dwelling, the tent of meeting.
Put the chest of the tablets inside, and hang the curtain in front of it to screen it from view.
Bring in the table and lay out the items that go on it. Then carry in the lampstand and mount the lamps on it.
Set the gold incense altar in front of the chest of the tablets, and hang the screen at the dwelling’s entrance.
The altar of burnt offering goes in front of the entrance of the dwelling, the tent of meeting.
Between the tent of meeting and the altar, place the washbasin and fill it with water.
Enclose the whole area with the courtyard, and hang the screen across its gate.
After that, take the anointing oil and sprinkle it over the dwelling and everything inside. Dedicate it and all its furnishings, and they will become holy.
Anoint the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils too. Dedicate the altar, and it will become most holy.
Anoint the basin and its stand as well, and dedicate them.
Next, have Aaron and his sons come to the entrance of the tent of meeting, where you will wash them in water.
Clothe Aaron in the holy garments, anoint him, and set him apart for his work as my priest.
Then have his sons step up, and put tunics on them.
Anoint them in the same way you anointed their father, so they can also act as my priests. By this anointing, their family becomes a priesthood for all the generations ahead.”
Moses did all of this exactly as Yahweh had ordered him.
The dwelling was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year after the Israelites left Egypt.{b}
Moses set up the dwelling by placing the bases, standing up the frames, fitting in the crossbars, and raising the posts.
He spread the tent over the dwelling and laid its covering on top, as Yahweh had ordered him.
He took the tablets and put them inside the chest. He attached the poles to the chest and set the cover on top of it.
He carried the chest into the dwelling and hung the screening curtain, so that it hid the chest of the tablets, as Yahweh had ordered him.
In the tent of meeting, on the north side of the dwelling and outside the curtain, Moses placed the table.
He arranged the bread on it before Yahweh, as Yahweh had ordered him.
Also in the tent of meeting, on the south side of the dwelling across from the table, he put the lampstand.
He lit the lamps in Yahweh’s presence, as Yahweh had ordered him.
In front of the curtain, in the tent of meeting, Moses set the gold altar.
On it he burned fragrant incense, as Yahweh had ordered him.
Then he hung the screen at the entrance of the dwelling.
Near the entrance of the dwelling, the tent of meeting, he placed the altar of burnt offering. On it he offered the burnt offering and the grain offering, as Yahweh had ordered him.
He positioned the basin between the tent of meeting and the altar, and poured in water for the priests’ washing.
Moses, Aaron, and Aaron’s sons would rinse their hands and feet in it.
Every time they entered the tent of meeting or went up to the altar, they washed, as Yahweh had ordered Moses.
Finally Moses erected the courtyard so that it surrounded the dwelling and the altar, and placed the screen across its gate. That finished the work.
Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and Yahweh’s glory filled the dwelling.
Moses was unable to enter the tent of meeting, because the cloud had settled{c} on it and Yahweh’s glory filled the dwelling.
At every stage of the journey, when the cloud lifted from over the dwelling, the Israelites would pack up and set out.
When the cloud stayed put, they stayed too, until the day it lifted.
During the day the cloud of Yahweh was over the dwelling, and at night there was fire in the cloud.{d} All the people of Israel could see it, throughout their journey.

notes.text: Hebrew “On the first day of the first month,” that is, Abib or Nisan, the first month of the spring-start religious calendar. It fell in March–April. See the note at 12:2.

Hebrew “In the first month in the second year, on the first of the month,” that is, the first day of Abib or Nisan (see the note at 12:2), almost a year after the exodus (12:6; 19:1). The Septuagint adds “after they went out of Egypt.”
Hebrew shakan, “to dwell,” the verb from which mishkan, “tabernacle,” comes (see the note at 25:9). Later Jewish tradition spoke of God’s dwelling presence as the Shekhinah.
Or “in the cloud.”
